classes.name: DeviceEnumerator
classes.summary: Cross-platform device enumerator that discovers and manages audio/video input devices, professional hardware, and network sources across all supported platforms.
classes.remarks: This class provides unified access to a wide variety of media devices: Standard webcams and video capture devicesMicrophones and audio capture sourcesAudio output devices (speakers, headphones, etc.)IP cameras via ONVIF protocolNDI (Network Device Interface) sources for IP video streamingBlackmagic Design DeckLink professional video hardwareIndustrial cameras supporting GenICam/GigE Vision standardsAllied Vision, Basler, and FLIR/Teledyne machine vision cameras The class supports both synchronous and asynchronous device discovery methods with platform-specific optimizations for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android. Real-time device change notifications are provided through events when devices are added or removed from the system. Use the singleton instance for most scenarios to avoid resource duplication and ensure consistent device state across your application.

properties.name: Video_IncludeMediaFoundation
properties.summary: Windows-only opt-in. When set to true, video-source enumeration also probes the Media Foundation device provider (mfdeviceprovider) in addition to Kernel Streaming. This exposes MF-only virtual cameras (NDI Webcam, OBS Virtual Camera, vendor virtual cameras, etc.) in the device list. Defaults to false. NVENC is no longer at risk. This flag was introduced because probing mfdeviceprovider used to break NvEncOpenEncodeSessionEx with NV_ENC_ERR_INVALID_VERSION for the rest of the process. The cause was not Media Foundation initialization: loading the mediafoundation plugin activated NVIDIA's Media Foundation encoder MFTs while registering its elements, and that activation is what invalidated later NVENC sessions. The Windows redistributables ship a patched plugin that excludes those MFTs, so enumerating MF devices and using nvh264enc/nvh265enc/nvav1enc in one process is safe — while the SDK loads its own runtime from the VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.* package. An application that resolves GStreamer from a stock installation on PATH / GST_PLUGIN_PATH instead gets the unpatched plugin, and with it the original failure. It stays opt-in because MF enumeration is additive rather than exclusive: cameras that are visible to both stacks are reported twice, once per API. Real KS-registered cameras (USB webcams, BRIO, most capture cards) are already covered by the default KS-only path, so turn this on when the application needs MF-only virtual cameras. The flag must be set BEFORE the first call to / ; it is not cached, so the enumerator reads it fresh on every call.

methods.name: StartAudioSourceMonitorInternal
methods.summary: Starts the audio source monitor and fills the device list, without announcing completion.
methods.remarks: The step EnumerateAudioSources takes when it needs a running monitor. Its caller owns the completion event, because only the caller knows whether the list is finished. Returns the started monitor, or null when the instance was disposed mid-start.

methods.name: StartAudioSourceMonitorCore
methods.summary: Recreates the audio source device monitor and starts it.
methods.remarks: Nothing that can block on hardware or on a permission dialog runs here: the providers start on their own thread from GStreamer 1.28 on, and the list is filled by the DeviceAdded messages the bus watch already handles, so the process-wide monitor lock is held only for create-and-start.
methods.returns: The start to wait on and to read the device list against, or null when the instance was disposed and no monitor was created.

methods.name: FinishAudioSourceMonitorStart
methods.summary: Completes an audio source monitor start with the devices the monitor cannot report.
methods.remarks: The snapshot runs on every start, not only when the monitor-started message failed to arrive: a GstDeviceProvider is a process-wide singleton, and starting one that another monitor already started increments its use count and posts nothing (gstdeviceprovider.c:468), so a second enumerator in the process would see the started message and not a single DeviceAdded. Waiting for that message first is what keeps the snapshot cheap: from GStreamer 1.28.3 on the Devices getter blocks until the provider start thread finishes - on macOS, behind the microphone permission dialog - and this method holds the process-wide monitor lock while it reads.

parameters.name: start
parameters.summary: The start whose monitor to read. May be null.

methods.name: AddAudioFilterWithoutKsDeviceProvider
methods.summary: Adds an audio filter to a monitor without letting ksdeviceprovider join it.
methods.remarks: The KS provider's klass claims Audio, so the filter would pick it, but it only enumerates cameras - and opening them raises the camera consent prompt in packaged apps (#2881). GstDeviceMonitor cannot exclude a provider, and no class or caps filter leaves this klass out. It takes only providers ranked above NONE, so the rank is dropped while the filter resolves them and put back right after. The factory stays in the registry: the camera lists find it by name without this lock, and a plugin load in the window must update it, not replace it. Every monitor start in this class holds around its filter, so none of them sees the dropped rank; a monitor built outside the enumerator in that window would. The lock is re-entrant for callers that already hold it.

methods.name: SaveDecklinkDeviceProvider
methods.summary: Saves the Decklink device provider reference so it can be loaded/unloaded on demand. The Decklink provider is unloaded by default to prevent interference with standard device enumeration and only loaded when explicitly enumerating Decklink-specific devices.

methods.name: LoadDecklinkDeviceProvider
methods.summary: Loads the Decklink device provider into the GStreamer registry, enabling Decklink-specific device enumeration for professional capture cards.

methods.name: UnloadDecklinkDeviceProvider
methods.summary: Unloads the Decklink device provider from the GStreamer registry. This prevents Decklink devices from appearing in standard device monitors and keeps them isolated to dedicated Decklink enumeration methods.

methods.name: IsStandardDriverDecklinkDevice
methods.summary: Determines whether a Blackmagic device registered through the Decklink GStreamer provider actually uses standard USB/UVC drivers instead of the proprietary Decklink SDK. ATEM switchers (ATEM Mini, ATEM Mini Pro, ATEM Mini Extreme, etc.) and Web Presenter devices present themselves as standard webcam/audio devices via USB-C and should appear in regular device listings rather than being routed through Decklink-specific pipelines.

parameters.name: displayName
parameters.summary: The GStreamer device display name to check (case-insensitive).

methods.returns: true if the device uses standard drivers; otherwise, false.

methods.name: IsDecklinkDevice
methods.summary: Returns true when the supplied Device originated from the GStreamer decklinkdeviceprovider. Centralized predicate used across the audio/video source/sink enumeration paths.
methods.remarks: Two-stage detection so this works across gst-plugins-bad versions: Fast path: device.Name contains the auto-generated "decklinkdevice" marker.Fallback: the device has a properties Structure with the decklink-specific signature fields (model-name + device-number), which the decklink device provider sets on every device it constructs (real Decklink hardware as well as ATEM and Web Presenter models — those are excluded separately via ). The property fallback is what covers a device whose name was set explicitly by whoever constructed it, which the marker cannot match.

methods.name: AddDeviceByProvider

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Releases all resources used by the DeviceEnumerator instance.
methods.remarks: This method stops all active device monitors, releases GStreamer resources, and unregisters any platform-specific device notification handlers. On Windows, this also stops the WMI event watcher used for USB device change notifications. After calling this method, the device enumerator cannot be reused. If using the instance, a new instance will be created automatically on the next access.

methods.name: ArmMonitorStart
methods.summary: Publishes a fresh monitor start, releasing whatever was in flight before it.
methods.remarks: The replaced start is released rather than disposed: a caller may still be inside Wait on its latch, and disposing under a waiter throws. Releasing it wakes that caller, which is what we want - its monitor is gone, and the device-list read it goes on to do recognises that and leaves the list to whoever replaced it.

parameters.name: field
parameters.summary: The start field paired with the monitor being started.

parameters.name: expectStartedMessage
parameters.summary: Whether this monitor can report through its bus.

methods.returns: The start to wait on and to read the device list against.

methods.name: ReleaseMonitorStart
methods.summary: Releases the in-flight monitor start exactly once and clears the field.
methods.remarks: Claiming the field before releasing is what makes this safe to call from the bus thread, from a competing start and from teardown at the same time: a SemaphoreSlim with a maximum count of one throws on a second Release, and only the thread that wins the exchange gets to release.

parameters.name: field
parameters.summary: The start field to release. May already be null.

methods.name: ReleaseMonitorStartFrom
methods.summary: Releases the in-flight monitor start, but only if it is the one this bus belongs to.
methods.remarks: A bus watch is removed while a callback for it may already be running on the main loop thread, so a message from the monitor a start has just replaced can arrive after the replacement was published. Matching the bus keeps that stale message from being read as "the new monitor's providers are up".

parameters.summary: The start field paired with the monitor.

parameters.summary: The bus that delivered the monitor-started message.

methods.summary: Adds a bus watch to a device monitor and records ownership of it.
methods.remarks: The watch's GSource attaches to the default main context and holds a reference on the bus plus a GCHandle on the delegate wrapper - which roots this enumerator until the watch is removed. Every add must be paired with exactly one guarded remove in teardown (#851).

methods.name: StopAndDisposeMonitor
methods.summary: Removes this enumerator's bus watch from a device monitor, stops it before releasing it, and clears the field.
methods.remarks: gst_device_monitor_dispose asserts '!self->priv->started', so disposing a monitor that was started logs a critical and leaves the provider's probe running. Stop() first. The watch comes off BEFORE Stop()/Dispose(): neither destroys it, and while it lives it pins the bus and keeps this instance rooted from the default main context (#851). Interlocked.Exchange makes the remove-exactly-once pairing race-safe.

methods.name: NDISourcesAsync
methods.summary: Asynchronously gets an array of available NDI video/audio sources on the network.
methods.remarks: This method discovers NDI sources available on the local network. NDI (Network Device Interface) is a royalty-free protocol for live video streaming over IP networks, commonly used in professional broadcast and video production environments. NDI source discovery may take time depending on network conditions. On Android, macOS and Linux the enumeration retries with delays; on Windows a single find waits for the senders itself. Worst-case wait budget: on Android an attempt blocks inside libndi's find_wait_for_sources up to 5000 ms the first time in the process and up to 2000 ms after that. The retry loop runs at most three attempts and inserts a 500 ms delay between attempts when no source has been observed yet. Total worst-case ceiling is therefore 5000 + 2 * 2000 + 2 * 500 = 10000 ms on Android, spent off the caller's thread. On Windows a single NDI SDK find waits up to 5000 ms for the first sender, then reads the list once it has been quiet for 2.5 s. On macOS and Linux the GStreamer DeviceMonitor path drives libndi's mDNS find with no native timeout; a single wedged discovery attempt is now bounded to NDI_DESKTOP_ENUM_TIMEOUT_MS (5000 ms), after which the call breaks out and returns the last-known/empty snapshot rather than blocking the caller forever. Use the overload if the caller needs to abort the worst-case wait early (e.g. when the user navigates away from a settings dialog).
methods.returns: A task that represents the asynchronous operation. The task result contains an array of NDISourceInfo objects representing available NDI sources.

methods.name: NDISourcesAsync
methods.summary: Asynchronously gets an array of available NDI video/audio sources, with cancellation support.

parameters.name: cancellationToken
parameters.summary: Cancellation token observed between retry attempts and during the inter-attempt back-off. The native libndi find_wait_for_sources blocking call cannot itself be interrupted mid-call; cancellation latency is therefore bounded by the per-attempt wait window (up to 5000 ms on Android, about 100 ms on Windows, near-instant on macOS and Linux) plus the 500 ms back-off when applicable.

methods.returns: A task that completes with the discovered sources, or faults with OperationCanceledException if cancellation fires.

methods.name: StartNDISourceWatch
methods.summary: Starts the background watcher that polls libndi for NDI source changes and fires NDISourcesChanged when the network set changes. Idempotent — calling twice with no intervening StopNDISourceWatch is a no-op for the second call.
methods.remarks: On Android the watcher reuses the persistent libndi find instance created by NDISourcesAsync, so subscribers see the same warm mDNS state callers of the snapshot API see. The first notification fires after the cold-start window (NDI_FIND_INITIAL_WAIT_MS, ~5 s) if it hasn't already happened.

methods.name: StopNDISourceWatch
methods.summary: Signals the background watcher to stop and waits briefly for it to exit. Safe to call when the watcher is not running.
methods.remarks: The watcher's tightest blocking call is find_wait_for_sources with a 10-second timeout, so worst-case Stop latency is ~10 s — but most stops resolve far faster because the wait short-circuits as soon as the source list moves. StopNDISourceWatch is also invoked automatically from Dispose so callers don't need to track lifetime themselves unless they want finer control.

methods.name: NDISourcesWindowsAsync
methods.summary: Lists NDI sources on Windows through the NDI SDK finder.
methods.remarks: Not through the GStreamer NDI device provider, for two measured reasons (#2655). Its monitor reports senders only seconds after it starts, so the snapshot taken right after the start was always empty. And it leaves an NDI find instance alive until process exit: in a process that has also created an NDI SDK receiver, libndi's DllMain then waits at exit for a worker the loader has already terminated, and the process never ends - not even on Stop-Process -Force. FinderSync keeps one finder for the process, and the NDI runtime destroys it before it is torn down at exit. One attempt is enough: the finder itself waits for the first sender.

parameters.name: cancellationToken
parameters.summary: Ends the find within one of its short waits.

methods.returns: The sources found.

methods.returns: The senders found; empty when there are none or no NDI runtime is installed.

methods.name: StartVideoSourceMonitorCore
methods.summary: Recreates the video source device monitor and starts it.
methods.remarks: Everything that can block on hardware or on a permission dialog is kept OUT of this method: GStreamer 1.28 starts the providers on its own thread, so the process-wide monitor lock is held only for the cheap create-and-start sequence, and the caller waits for the report with the lock free.

methods.name: PopulateVideoSourcesFromMonitor
methods.summary: Fills the video source list from a device-list snapshot taken off the monitor.
methods.remarks: Runs on every start, not only when the monitor-started message failed to arrive: a GstDeviceProvider is a process-wide singleton, and starting one that another monitor already started increments its use count and posts nothing (gstdeviceprovider.c:468). A second enumerator in the same process would therefore get the started message and not a single DeviceAdded, and its list would come back empty. Waiting for the started message first is what keeps this cheap and off the critical path: from GStreamer 1.28.3 on the Devices getter blocks until the provider start thread has finished - on macOS, behind the camera permission dialog - and this method holds the process-wide monitor lock while it reads. By the time the message has arrived the providers are up and the getter returns their cached lists.

classes.name: ColorspaceConverterX
classes.summary: Provides high-performance colorspace conversion for video frames using GStreamer.
classes.remarks: The ColorspaceConverterX class leverages GStreamer's videoconvert element to perform efficient colorspace transformations between different video formats. It supports: - Multiple input and output video formats (RGB, BGR, YUV, etc.) - Hardware-accelerated conversions when available - Thread-safe operation with internal synchronization - Configurable timeout for conversion operations The converter uses an internal GStreamer pipeline with appsrc and appsink elements to process frames in real-time. Each conversion operation is synchronized using an AutoResetEvent to ensure proper buffer handling. This class implements and must be properly disposed to release GStreamer resources and native memory.

constructors.name: ColorspaceConverterX
constructors.summary: Initializes a new instance of the ColorspaceConverterX class.
constructors.remarks: This constructor creates and configures a GStreamer pipeline with the following elements: - appsrc: Receives input frames - capsfilter (input): Enforces input format constraints - videoconvert: Performs the actual colorspace conversion - capsfilter (output): Enforces output format constraints - appsink: Provides converted output frames The pipeline is automatically started during construction. If initialization fails, all allocated resources are cleaned up and an exception is thrown.

parameters.name: context
parameters.summary: The base context for logging and error reporting. Can be null if logging is not required.

parameters.name: inputFormat
parameters.summary: The video format of the input frames (e.g., RGB, BGR, YUV).

parameters.name: outputFormat
parameters.summary: The desired video format for the output frames.

parameters.name: width
parameters.summary: The width of the video frames in pixels.

parameters.name: height
parameters.summary: The height of the video frames in pixels.

methods.name: StartPipeline
methods.summary: Starts the GStreamer pipeline and sets it to the playing state.

methods.name: Convert
methods.summary: Converts video frame data from the input colorspace to the output colorspace.
methods.remarks: This method performs a synchronous colorspace conversion operation: 1. Creates a GStreamer buffer from the input data 2. Pushes the buffer through the conversion pipeline 3. Waits for the converted output (with timeout) 4. Copies the result to the output buffer The operation is thread-safe and uses internal locking to ensure only one conversion happens at a time. If the pipeline is not started, it will be started automatically. If the conversion times out, no data is written to the output buffer and an error is logged.

parameters.name: outFrameData
parameters.summary: A pointer to the output frame data buffer that will receive the converted data.

parameters.name: outFrameDataSize
parameters.summary: The size of the output frame data buffer in bytes.

parameters.name: timeoutMs
parameters.summary: The maximum time to wait for conversion completion, in milliseconds. Default is 1000ms.

methods.name: Reset
methods.summary: Resets the colorspace converter pipeline and clears internal buffers.
methods.remarks: This method stops the GStreamer pipeline, restarts it, and releases all cached output buffers. Use this method if you need to recover from errors or clear the pipeline state. After reset, the converter is ready to process new frames.

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Performs application-defined tasks associated with freeing, releasing, or resetting unmanaged resources.
methods.remarks: This method stops the GStreamer pipeline, disconnects event handlers, and releases all native resources including GStreamer elements and allocated memory buffers. After calling Dispose, the converter instance cannot be reused. Consider using a 'using' statement to ensure proper disposal.

methods.name: Finalize
methods.summary: Finalizes an instance of the ColorspaceConverterX class and releases unmanaged resources.
methods.remarks: This destructor ensures that native resources are released even if Dispose is not called explicitly. For better performance and deterministic cleanup, always call Dispose explicitly.

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Releases the unmanaged and optionally the managed resources used by the ColorspaceConverterX class.
methods.remarks: On either path the allocated native memory for the output buffer is freed. When called from Dispose (disposing = true), this method also: - Disposes the buffer processed event - Stops the GStreamer pipeline - Disconnects event handlers to prevent callbacks after disposal - Disposes all GStreamer objects (bin, caps) From the finalizer (disposing = false) only the buffer is freed: GstSharp wrappers must not be touched here, so their native objects are released through the toggle-ref queued-unref path instead.

parameters.name: disposing
parameters.summary: If set to true, releases both managed and unmanaged resources; if false, releases only unmanaged resources.

classes.name: FFT
classes.summary: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) implementation for audio frequency analysis and spectrum computation. Provides high-performance FFT calculations for real-time audio processing, frequency analysis, and spectrum visualization within the VisioForge SDK. Based on the Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm with optimizations for power-of-two sample sizes commonly used in audio processing.

Interface Access: - Use GetInstance() to get the singleton GenTL interface - GenTL interface is automatically discovered by Aravis system - Available when GenTL producers are installed on the system 2. Device Discovery: - Use ArvInterface base methods for device enumeration - GenTL devices will be discovered through interface operations - Device IDs can be used with ArvGentlDevice.CreateDevice() 3. Interface Operations: - All standard interface operations available through ArvInterface.cs - GenTL-specific functionality integrated with base interface - Update device list and open device methods work with GenTL 4. System Integration: - GenTL interface works with ArvSystem enumeration - Appears in system interface list when available - Compatible with standard Aravis discovery patterns 5. Error Handling: - Check for IntPtr.Zero return values - GenTL errors follow standard GError pattern - Interface availability depends on GenTL producer installation

methods.name: ShowUsageExamples

methods.name: ShowIntegrationGuidance
methods.summary: Integration guidance for GenTL streams: 1. Stream Creation: - GenTL streams are created through GenTL device instances - Use ArvDevice.arv_device_create_stream() on GenTL devices - Stream creation handled by GenTL producer automatically 2. Stream Operations: - All standard stream operations available through ArvStream.cs - Buffer management through ArvBuffer.cs - Acquisition control through ArvStream start/stop methods 3. GenTL Features: - GenTL-specific optimizations handled transparently - Producer-specific buffer management automatic - Transport layer optimizations integrated 4. Buffer Handling: - Standard buffer operations through ArvBuffer.cs - GenTL buffer allocation handled by producer - Memory management follows standard patterns 5. Error Handling: - GenTL streams follow standard GError pattern - Stream-specific errors reported through standard mechanisms - Producer errors integrated with Aravis error handling 6. Performance: - GenTL producers may provide optimized streaming - Zero-copy operations where supported by producer - Hardware-specific optimizations automatic

methods.name: ShowUsageExamples
methods.summary: Example usage patterns for GenTL streams: // Create GenTL device and stream IntPtr gentlDevice = ArvGentlDevice.CreateDevice(system, "interfaceId", "deviceId"); IntPtr gentlStream = ArvDevice.CreateStream(gentlDevice, callback, userData); // Configure stream ArvStream.SetBufferSize(gentlStream, bufferSize); ArvStream.PushBuffer(gentlStream, buffer); // Start acquisition ArvStream.StartAcquisition(gentlStream); // Get frames IntPtr buffer = ArvStream.PopBuffer(gentlStream); if (buffer != IntPtr.Zero) { // Process frame data ProcessFrameData(buffer); // Return buffer to stream ArvStream.PushBuffer(gentlStream, buffer); } // Stop acquisition ArvStream.StopAcquisition(gentlStream); Note: This is pseudocode - actual implementation follows standard Aravis streaming patterns with GenTL integration.

methods.name: ShowProducerIntegration
methods.summary: GenTL Producer integration notes: 1. Producer Discovery: - GenTL producers automatically discovered by Aravis - Multiple producers can coexist on the system - Producer selection handled by GenTL system 2. Stream Capabilities: - Producer-specific streaming features automatically available - Hardware acceleration where supported - Transport-specific optimizations integrated 3. Buffer Management: - Producer-optimized buffer allocation - Zero-copy operations where possible - Memory mapping for performance 4. Configuration: - Producer-specific parameters accessible through GenICam - Transport layer configuration through device interface - Streaming parameters through standard Aravis API 5. Compatibility: - Standard Aravis API maintained for compatibility - GenTL features accessible through existing interfaces - Transparent integration with Aravis ecosystem

System Initialization: - GenTL systems are typically initialized through ArvSystem.cs - Use ArvSystem interface enumeration to discover GenTL interfaces - GenTL system instances are managed internally by Aravis 2. Interface Discovery: - Use ArvSystem.arv_system_get_interfaces() to enumerate interfaces - GenTL interfaces will be included in the interface list - Use ArvGentlInterface for GenTL-specific interface operations 3. classes.name: GenICamCamera
classes.summary: Represents a GenICam-compliant camera device with high-level access to camera information, resolutions, pixel formats, and control features. This class provides a comprehensive wrapper around the Aravis library for industrial camera control. Typical Usage Workflow:Create camera instance using Call to establish connectionCall to populate camera capabilitiesConfigure camera settings (exposure, gain, ROI, etc.)Use for continuous capture or for single shotsHandle events for frame processingCall and when doneThread Safety: This class is not thread-safe. Access should be synchronized when used from multiple threads, particularly for streaming operations. Resource Management: The class implements . Always dispose of camera instances when done, either explicitly or using 'using' statements. Alternatively, use for temporary disconnection without disposal. Basic usage example: using var camera = GenICamCameraManager.GetCamera("MyCamera"); if (camera.Connect()) { camera.ReadInfo(); camera.SetExposureTime(10000); // 10ms camera.SetGain(0.0); camera.FrameReceived += (s, e) => { Console.WriteLine($"Frame: {e.FrameData.Width}x{e.FrameData.Height}"); }; camera.StartStreaming(); Thread.Sleep(5000); // Stream for 5 seconds camera.StopStreaming(); } API Update Notes: - Fixed acquisition startup sequence: camera acquisition handles device-level streaming automatically - Removed redundant arv_stream_start_acquisition calls that could conflict with camera acquisition - Updated buffer management to use modern Aravis buffer management APIs - Enhanced stream diagnostics with FillingBuffers parameter support - Improved error handling and logging throughout streaming operations - Added pre-flight checks for camera and stream handles before starting acquisition

classes.name: GenICamCameraManager
classes.summary: Static class for centralized camera management and enumeration of GenICam-compatible cameras. This class provides centralized management and enumeration of GenICamCamera instances to ensure: - Each camera is created only once and reused across the application - Simple open/closed state tracking with thread-safe operations - Thread-safe access to camera instances using concurrent collections - Automatic cleanup when cameras are no longer needed or available - Comprehensive device enumeration and discovery with real-time updates - Proper resource management and disposal patterns Thread Safety: This class is fully thread-safe and can be used from multiple threads simultaneously.Usage Pattern:Call to populate the camera dictionary with available devicesUse to get a camera reference by device IDCall before using the camera for operationsPerform camera operations (streaming, configuration, etc.)Call when done with the cameraResource Management:Cameras are automatically cleaned up when they become unavailable. The manager tracks device availability and removes cameras that are no longer present in the system during calls. // Enumerate and populate camera dictionary GenICamCameraManager.UpdateDeviceList(); // Get camera reference var camera = GenICamCameraManager.GetCamera("MyCamera"); if (camera == null) { Console.WriteLine("Camera not found"); return; } // Open camera for use if (GenICamCameraManager.OpenCamera("MyCamera")) { try { // Use camera for operations camera.StartStreaming(); // Perform image capture operations // ... do work ... camera.StopStreaming(); } finally { // Always close camera when done GenICamCameraManager.CloseCamera("MyCamera"); } } else { Console.WriteLine("Failed to open camera"); }

methods.name: SetContext
methods.summary: Sets the BaseContext for logging operations throughout the camera manager.
methods.remarks: This method should be called early in the application lifecycle to ensure proper logging throughout camera operations.

parameters.name: context
parameters.summary: BaseContext instance for logging. If null, a new default context will be created.

methods.name: UpdateDeviceList
methods.summary: Updates the device list by scanning for available GenICam-compatible cameras. Automatically cleans up cameras that are no longer available in the system.
methods.remarks: This method performs the following operations:Calls the underlying Aravis system to refresh the device listCompares current devices with cached camera instancesRemoves cameras that are no longer available (if not connected)Adds new cameras to the internal dictionaryThread Safety: This method is thread-safe and can be called from multiple threads.Performance: This method may take some time to complete as it performs hardware enumeration. Consider calling it on a background thread in UI applications.

methods.name: PopulateCameraDictionary
methods.summary: Populates the camera dictionary with discovered cameras without connecting to them.
methods.remarks: This is an internal method that creates GenICamCamera instances for each discovered device and adds them to the internal cache. The cameras are not connected at this stage.

methods.name: GetDeviceCount
methods.summary: Gets the number of currently available GenICam-compatible devices.
methods.remarks: This method returns the count from the most recent device enumeration. Call UpdateDeviceList to refresh the device list before calling this method if you need the most up-to-date count.
methods.returns: The number of available cameras detected by the system.

methods.name: GetDeviceIds
methods.summary: Gets device IDs for all currently available GenICam-compatible cameras.
methods.remarks: This method automatically calls to ensure the most current device list.Device IDs are typically in the format "Vendor_Model_SerialNumber" but the exact format depends on the camera manufacturer.The returned array will contain "Unknown" for devices where the ID cannot be determined.
methods.returns: An array of device ID strings. Each string uniquely identifies a camera device.

methods.name: GetDeviceId
methods.summary: Gets the device ID for a specific camera by its enumeration index.
methods.remarks: This method automatically calls to ensure the most current device list.Device indices are assigned in the order devices are discovered and may change between enumerations.

parameters.name: index
parameters.summary: The zero-based index of the device in the enumeration list.

methods.returns: The device ID string for the specified camera, or "Unknown" if the ID cannot be determined.

methods.name: GetCamera
methods.summary: Gets a camera instance by device ID, creating it if necessary but not connecting to it.
methods.remarks: This method returns a camera instance from the internal cache. If the camera doesn't exist in the cache, it will attempt to create a new instance. The camera is not automatically connected.Important: You must call before using this method to ensure the device is available in the enumerated list.Use to connect to the camera before performing operations.

parameters.name: deviceId
parameters.summary: The unique device ID of the camera to retrieve.

methods.returns: A GenICamCamera instance for the specified device, or null if the device ID is invalid or the camera cannot be created.

methods.name: GetCameraInternal
methods.summary: Internal method to get or create camera instances with proper recreation logic. Handles camera reinitialization when needed.
methods.remarks: This method handles the complex logic of camera lifecycle management including: - Checking if the camera exists in the enumerated device list - Attempting to reinitialize disposed cameras - Creating new camera instances when needed - Proper error handling and logging

parameters.name: deviceId
parameters.summary: The unique device ID of the camera to retrieve.

methods.returns: A GenICamCamera instance or null if the camera cannot be created or retrieved.

methods.name: GetCamera
methods.summary: Gets a camera instance by its enumeration index.
methods.remarks: This method is a convenience wrapper that gets the device ID for the specified index and then retrieves the corresponding camera instance.Note: Device indices may change between enumerations. For consistent access, consider using device IDs instead of indices.

parameters.name: index
parameters.summary: The zero-based index of the camera in the device enumeration.

methods.returns: A GenICamCamera instance for the camera at the specified index.

methods.name: GetCameras
methods.summary: Gets all available cameras as GenICamCamera instances from the centralized cache.
methods.remarks: This method retrieves camera instances for all devices found in the most recent enumeration. Cameras that cannot be created or retrieved are skipped with a warning logged.The returned cameras are not automatically connected. Use to connect to individual cameras before use.Performance: This method may take some time if there are many cameras or if some cameras are slow to respond during instantiation.
methods.returns: A list of GenICamCamera instances for all available cameras. Cameras that cannot be retrieved are excluded from the list.

methods.name: GetFirstAvailableCamera
methods.summary: Gets the first available camera from the centralized cache.
methods.remarks: This is a convenience method for applications that only need to work with a single camera or want to use the first available camera by default.This method automatically calls to ensure current device information.The returned camera is not automatically connected. Use to connect to the camera before use.
methods.returns: A GenICamCamera instance for the first available camera.

methods.name: OpenCamera
methods.summary: Opens a camera for use by establishing a connection to the hardware.
methods.remarks: This method performs the following operations:Validates the device ID and retrieves the camera instanceChecks if the camera is already connected (returns true if so)Establishes a hardware connection to the cameraReads camera information to populate detailed propertiesThread Safety: This method is thread-safe and uses internal locking.Resource Management: Always call when done with the camera to properly release resources.Error Handling: Detailed error information is logged. Check logs for specific failure reasons.

parameters.name: deviceId
parameters.summary: The unique device ID of the camera to open.

methods.returns: true if the camera was successfully opened and is ready for use; false if the camera could not be opened.

methods.name: CloseCamera
methods.summary: Closes a camera and disconnects it from the hardware without removing it from the cache.
methods.remarks: This method performs the following operations:Stops any active streaming on the cameraDisconnects the camera from the hardwareKeeps the camera instance in cache for potential reuseThread Safety: This method is thread-safe and uses internal locking.Resource Management: This method properly releases hardware resources while maintaining the camera instance for future use.Idempotent: It's safe to call this method multiple times on the same camera.

parameters.name: deviceId
parameters.summary: The unique device ID of the camera to close.

methods.returns: true if the camera was successfully closed or was already closed; false if an error occurred during the closing process.

methods.name: IsCameraOpen
methods.summary: Checks if a camera is currently open and connected to the hardware.
methods.remarks: This method provides a quick way to check camera connection status without attempting to open or modify the camera state.Thread Safety: This method is thread-safe and can be called from any thread.Performance: This is a lightweight operation that only checks internal state.

parameters.name: deviceId
parameters.summary: The unique device ID of the camera to check.

methods.returns: true if the camera is currently open and connected; false if the camera is closed, not found, or the device ID is invalid.

methods.name: ForceCleanup
methods.summary: Forces removal and disposal of all cameras from the cache, regardless of their current state.
methods.remarks: ⚠️ WARNING: This method should be used with extreme caution as it will dispose all camera instances even if they are currently in use. This can cause exceptions in other parts of the application that are actively using cameras.This method is intended for use in the following scenarios:Application shutdownRecovery from unrecoverable camera statesMemory cleanup in testing scenariosThread Safety: This method is thread-safe but will affect all threads using cameras.Recovery: After calling this method, you must call to repopulate the camera cache before using cameras again.

methods.name: FindCamerasByVendor
methods.summary: Finds cameras by vendor name using case-insensitive partial matching.
methods.remarks: This method performs a case-insensitive search for cameras whose vendor name contains the specified string. Partial matches are supported.Performance: This method may take some time as it needs to query device information for each available camera.Cameras that cannot be queried are skipped with a warning logged.

parameters.name: vendorName

classes.name: DSPAudioEffectFilter
classes.summary: Runs one managed DSP effect of DSP on the audio stream of a GStreamer pipeline. GitHub issue #3697.
classes.remarks: The graph is audioconvert ! capsfilter(F64LE) ! audioconvert ! capsfilter(F32LE, interleaved) ! audioconvert. The effect rewrites buffers in place from a pad probe on the F32LE capsfilter, and a buffer something else still references - a tee upstream, for one - cannot be mapped for writing. A probe cannot swap the buffer either: PadProbeInfo reaches managed code as a copy. F64LE to F32LE changes the sample size, so that convert always outputs a new buffer only this chain holds. The last audioconvert gives the elements downstream the format they negotiate.

methods.summary: Processes one buffer in place, on the streaming thread.

methods.summary: Applies the settings of effect to the DSP effect.

parameters.summary: The effect, of the type that goes with this filter's ID.

methods.name: ReportPendingError
methods.summary: Reports what the filter found from the thread pool. The application's OnError handler may run right where the error is raised, and it must be free to wait for its UI thread or to stop the pipeline: neither works on the streaming thread the stop waits for, or under the effect block's lock, which a setter on that UI thread needs.

methods.name: ApplySettings
methods.summary: Maps the public settings onto the DSP effect. Runs under _dspLock.
methods.remarks: TrueBass and TrebleEnhancer compute the coefficient of their state-variable filter as sin(pi * f / rate), and the corner of that filter sits where 2 * sin(pi * fc / rate) equals it, so they cut well below the frequency they are given; UInt32) solves that. ponytail: the coefficient tops out at 1, so no corner goes above a sixth of the sample rate (8 kHz at 48 kHz). A higher one needs a different filter design.

methods.name: ToCornerValue
methods.summary: The value that puts a filter's corner at hz. A frequency above the limit of the filter design works at that limit, and the first one reports an error.

Passing a linear double let GLib transform it silently, so the SDK default of 0.05 arrived as 0 dB - full scale, where practically every sample reads as silence. The conversion happens here so the public API can stay linear. The element then keeps whole decades of the dB value, truncating toward zero (power = (gint)(db / 10.0)), so -65 dB and -60 dB both apply as -60 dB.

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.summary: The threshold value as a linear value (0.0 to 1.0).

methods.name: LinearToThresholdDb
methods.summary: Converts a linear amplitude into the integer dB value the removesilence element expects.

parameters.name: linear
parameters.summary: A linear amplitude; anything at or below zero maps to the quietest threshold.

methods.returns: The threshold in dB, clamped to the element's -70..70 range.

methods.name: SetSquash

parameters.name: squash
parameters.summary: true to close the gap left by removed silence; false to keep the original timeline.

methods.name: DetachRTCPLegsFromEosTally
methods.summary: Takes the RTCP legs out of the bin's End-Of-Stream tally, so that stopping a RIST output reaches EOS instead of burning the pipeline's whole graceful-EOS budget.
methods.remarks: ristsink is a bin holding two udpsinks per bond - the RTP one and an RTCP one - and gst_bin_iterate_sinks() counts both, so the bin posts EOS only after both have. The RTCP leg never can: rtpsession pushes EOS on send_rtcp_src only once every internal source has sent a BYE (rtpsession.c: rtp_session_are_all_sources_bye), a BYE is only written by make_source_bye, and generate_rtcp returns early for a source with RTCP disabled - which is what ristsink does to its own retransmission SSRC (gstristsink.c: gst_rist_sink_on_new_sender_ssrc). The RTP leg does reach EOS, so dropping the sink flag on the RTCP leg makes the tally depend on the leg that can answer it. Data flow is untouched - RTCP keeps flowing exactly as before, only the end-of-stream bookkeeping changes. Issue #1463.

methods.name: GetLaunchString
methods.summary: Builds the encoder fragment of the gst_parse_launch string for an H264 settings object.
methods.remarks: Media Foundation encoders are special-cased (issue #858): their element classes install properties only when the MFT advertises support, so a launch string carrying more than bitrate can fail to parse outright on a host that exposes less — and the RTSP media then never constructs. Only the unconditionally-present property goes into the string; everything else is applied by OnMediaConfigure once the real element exists. NVENC is handled the same way, with only the element name in the string (issue #2842).

methods.name: GetLaunchString
methods.summary: HEVC counterpart of IH264EncoderSettings).

methods.name: ConnectMediaConfigure
methods.summary: Connects IntPtr) through a raw callback. The managed MediaConfigure event would wrap the GstRTSPMedia argument, and that wrapper keeps the media - and the whole encoder bin - alive after the server is gone, until a GC (#2214).

methods.name: OnMediaConfigure
methods.summary: Applies the full Media Foundation or NVENC encoder settings to the element the RTSP media factory created from the launch string. Runs after gst_parse_launch and before the media leaves NULL, which is the first point where the real element - with its machine-specific property set - exists. Every property goes through EncoderHelpers.TrySetProperty, so one the MFT or the GPU does not support is skipped with a warning instead of failing anything.

methods.summary: Depth-first search for an element whose name starts with one of the prefixes; calls apply on the first one while its wrapper is still valid.
methods.returns: true when an element was found.

methods.name: BuildAudioPipeline
methods.summary: Builds the audio pipeline string based on the settings.
methods.returns: The audio pipeline string.

methods.name: GetBridgeVideoFormat
methods.summary: The raw video format carried through the inter-video bridge.
methods.remarks: RGB is the common denominator every encoder here can be fed from. It carries no alpha, so an encoder asked to keep an alpha channel would receive a fully opaque one and encode it in silence. RGBA for that case only - it costs one channel through the bridge and nothing else in this graph asks for it. Main 10 widens it the same way and for the same reason: RGB is 8-bit, so a bridge left at RGB would flatten the source to 8 bits one element before a filter that pins P010_10LE, and the stream would be labelled Main 10 while carrying nothing a Main profile could not. Both ends of the bridge read this. Pinning only the read side would flatten the alpha on the way in and then re-add an opaque channel on the way out, which looks like a fix and is not.

methods.summary: The caps both ends of the video bridge use: the input links with them, the media factory reads them.

methods.summary: Adds a converter and an inter sink on channel to the pipeline and links them through capsStr. On failure the pipeline removes what was added.

methods.name: RequestStop
methods.summary: Signals the sink that the pipeline is stopping. Disables the native sink's auto-reconnect so a streaming thread parked in the reconnect loop against an unreachable peer exits promptly and StopAsync is not blocked. The prompt exit needs a native SRT plugin that honors a mid-flight switch-off; the macOS redist ships a patched libgstsrt.dylib (#879), the Windows redist a patched gstsrt.dll (#1190), and the Android and iOS redists a patched srt plugin built into libgstreamer_android.so (#1350) and GStreamerX.framework (#1349). Stock GStreamer builds capture the setting once per read/write call, so the loop ends only from the next call.

methods.name: SetHostAndPort
methods.summary: Redirects the sink at runtime.
methods.remarks: It exists so the muxer sinks and the block layer that own a UDPSink can push these two without reaching through _sink.Element. The static SetElementProperty overload takes no lock and asks its caller to hold SyncRoot across the read and the push - which a foreign type cannot do, because SyncRoot is protected. Pushing from in here does hold it. GitHub issue #948. One lock across both, not the instance overload twice: a second caller retargeting the sink between the two pushes would leave udpsink at one caller's host and the other's port, and it re-reads both per buffer, so packets go to that address until something pushes again.

methods.name: RelabelSideToRear
methods.summary: Relabels 5.0/5.1 with side surrounds (SL/SR, e.g. decoded AC-3) as rear surrounds (RL/RR). Side layouts are not AAC channel configurations, so the encoder signals them with a PCE and channel_config 0; MPEG-TS/HLS carries AAC as ADTS, which keeps the 0 and drops the PCE, and no decoder can open the stream (#2182). Rear layouts map to configurations 5 and 6. SL/SR are the last two channels in both masks, so RL/RR take the same positions and no sample changes.

methods.remarks: vorbisenc declares bitrate, max-bitrate and min-bitrate as Integer, range -1 to 250001, where -1 means disabled - which is also the default of all three settings. Scaling that default produced -1000, GLib rejected the assignment as out of range, and the encoder silently kept its own default: every bitrate the caller set was applied only if they had also overridden the sentinel. The same value reaches the encoding profile structure, so the profile carried the invalid number too.

classes.name: BridgeAudioTrace
classes.summary: Diagnostic tracer used while debugging the live-mixer / app-bridge audio path. All public methods are decorated with ConditionalAttribute targeting the BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE compile-time symbol — when the symbol is NOT defined in the calling assembly, the C# compiler elides the call site entirely and the tracer carries zero runtime cost (no AutoInit, no file IO, no thread). To enable tracing in a project, add BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE to that project's DefineConstants and rebuild. Property accesses (Enabled, CurrentPath, CurrentInfoPath) cannot be elided by ConditionalAttribute; consumers must wrap those in #if BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE.

properties.name: Enabled
properties.summary: Gets or sets whether the tracer actively records buffer events. Set to true to enable tracing; defaults to false.

properties.name: CurrentPath
properties.summary: Gets the absolute path of the CSV trace file written by the background flush thread. null until the first call that triggers AutoInit.

properties.name: CurrentInfoPath
properties.summary: Gets the absolute path of the plain-text session info file that accompanies the CSV trace. null until the first call that triggers AutoInit.

methods.name: FlushNow
methods.summary: Forces an immediate flush of all pending trace rows to disk. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

methods.name: ResetProbeRegistry
methods.summary: Clears the internal registry of pads that already have buffer probes attached, allowing probes to be re-registered after a pipeline restart. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

methods.name: Log
methods.summary: Records a raw buffer-timing entry to the trace CSV. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

parameters.name: pts
parameters.summary: Buffer presentation timestamp in GStreamer nanoseconds.

parameters.name: dts
parameters.summary: Buffer decode timestamp in GStreamer nanoseconds.

parameters.name: size
parameters.summary: Buffer size in bytes, or -1 if unavailable.

parameters.name: queueBuffers
parameters.summary: Current number of buffers in the monitored queue, or -1 if unavailable.

parameters.name: queueBytes
parameters.summary: Current byte fill of the monitored queue, or -1 if unavailable.

parameters.name: queueTime
parameters.summary: Current time fill of the monitored queue in nanoseconds, or -1 if unavailable.

parameters.name: extra
parameters.summary: Optional free-form annotation appended to the row.

methods.name: LogBuffer
methods.summary: Records timing and size information from a GStreamer Buffer to the trace CSV. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

parameters.name: buffer
parameters.summary: The GStreamer buffer whose timestamps and size are recorded.

parameters.name: queueElement
parameters.summary: Optional queue element whose fill levels are sampled.

methods.name: LogSample
methods.summary: Records timing and size information from a GStreamer Sample to the trace CSV. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

parameters.name: sample
parameters.summary: The GStreamer sample whose buffer timestamps and size are recorded.

methods.name: LogInfo
methods.summary: Records a plain informational entry (zero timestamps, no buffer) to the trace CSV. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

parameters.name: location
parameters.summary: Code location tag or message label.

methods.name: AppendSessionInfo
methods.summary: Appends a titled section to the plain-text session info file that accompanies the trace CSV. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

methods.name: LogQueue
methods.summary: Records the current fill levels of a GStreamer queue element to the trace CSV without associating a buffer. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

parameters.name: queueElement
parameters.summary: The queue element whose current-level properties are sampled.

methods.name: AddPadBufferProbe
methods.summary: Attaches a GStreamer pad buffer probe that automatically calls String) for every buffer passing through pad. A probe is only attached once per pad identity. Elided by the compiler when BRIDGE_AUDIO_TRACE is not defined in the caller.

parameters.name: stream
parameters.summary: Logical stream label used in trace rows emitted by the probe.

parameters.name: location
parameters.summary: Code location tag used in trace rows emitted by the probe.

parameters.name: queueElement
parameters.summary: Optional queue element whose fill levels are sampled on each buffer.

parameters.name: extra
parameters.summary: Optional free-form annotation appended to trace rows.

methods.name: RemoveBridgeSinkBlock
methods.summary: Removes the bridge sink registered under pairID, but only when that entry is still owner.
methods.remarks: The identity check is the point of the method: a key is not exclusive to whoever holds it now. A block registers itself in its constructor and its element overwrites that entry under the same key from Build(), the blocks expose a settable PairID, and nothing stops a second block being created with an id a previous one used. Removing blind by key then deletes somebody else's live registration and the bridge that owns it silently finds no peer - no exception, no log line, just no data.

parameters.summary: The object that registered under pairID.

classes.name: GstCriticalWatch
classes.summary: Watcher for GLib/GStreamer CRITICAL log messages.
classes.remarks: A GStreamer critical such as gst_element_set_state: assertion 'GST_IS_ELEMENT (element)' failed means a pointer handed to the C API did not pass a type check. GLib turns that into a no-op plus a log line, so the process survives — but the same call against a pointer that still happens to look like a live object is a use-after-free. Criticals are therefore worth failing a test over, not just logging. Every one of those calls is a P/Invoke made synchronously from managed code, so the MANAGED stack at the moment the critical fires names the exact call site. A native backtrace cannot: the JIT-compiled frames come back unsymbolicated. That is what captures. Nothing is installed until one of two callers asks. The test suite calls , which installs the handlers and keeps every critical for . An application switches on the Debug_NativeCriticals property of an SDK engine or a MediaBlocksPipeline (), which installs the same handlers with stack capture and routes every critical to that component's OnError, and to a file in its Debug_Dir written immediately, so the lines preceding a crash survive it. The list is not kept for subscribers. Once installed the handlers stay until (with nobody subscribed) or : they replace GLib's default handler for the watched domains, and cost nothing until a critical fires.

properties.name: Count
properties.summary: Gets the number of criticals recorded since the last Reset, including any the retention cap dropped.

properties.name: SuppressedCount
properties.summary: Gets the number of criticals dropped as known upstream noise since the last Reset; see String). A non-zero value here with an empty GetMessages means the run was noisy and the noise was recognised, not that the watcher saw nothing.

properties.name: IsInstalled
properties.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the log handlers are installed. False means the watcher is recording nothing — a zero Count then proves nothing at all.

properties.name: Subscription.Reports
properties.summary: Gets or sets the criticals raised through this component's OnError so far; see MaxOnErrorReports. A fresh subscription starts a fresh budget.

properties.name: Subscription.InstallProblem
properties.summary: Gets or sets the setup problems this component was last told about; see String).

methods.name: GetMessages
methods.summary: Gets a snapshot of the criticals recorded since the last Reset, most recent last. Each entry is "<domain>: <message>".
methods.returns: A copy of the recorded messages; never null.

methods.name: Enable
methods.summary: Installs the log handlers and starts recording. Idempotent, so any number of test constructors may call it. Stack capture, once any call asks for it, stays on until Disable: a later call with the default argument never switches it off.

parameters.name: captureStacks
parameters.summary: When true, the managed stack trace of the offending thread is printed with every critical. That is what identifies the call site; leave it off for a quiet run that only counts.

methods.name: Install
methods.summary: Installs the handlers; see Boolean). Shared with InstallForSubscribers, which must not switch on recording. Idempotent: the first successful call installs them.

methods.name: OnBindingLifetimeReport
methods.summary: Records a lifetime defect the managed binding detected. Kept separate from String) because it is not a GLib message and has no domain or level.

methods.name: ReportInvariant
methods.summary: Records an SDK threading invariant broken in managed code - such as user code reached while an SDK lock is held (issue #1711) - so the test suite's guard fails the test that broke it. Always with the managed stack in the recorded message, since several regions log the same text.

methods.name: Disable
methods.summary: Ends the Boolean) caller's use: stops recording, drops what was recorded, and withdraws its stack request. The handlers are removed too, restoring GLib's own handling for the domains this type had claimed - unless a Debug_NativeCriticals subscriber still relies on them.

methods.name: Shutdown
methods.summary: Removes the handlers and closes the file whoever asked for them. Called by VisioForgeX.StopMainLoop, when the managed domain is about to unload while native GLib survives - Unity's assembly reload: a handler left installed would call into the unloaded domain on the next critical, the same dangling callback GstInitializer.DetachLogFunction removes for the GStreamer debug log. Not by DestroySDK: the domain, and the subscriptions, live on.

methods.name: RemoveHandlers
methods.summary: Removes the per-domain handlers, if installed. Caller holds _sync.

methods.name: SetSubscribed
methods.summary: Switches criticals reporting on or off for one component. Backs Debug_NativeCriticals.
methods.remarks: On: every later critical goes, with its managed stack, to the criticals file and through report to the component's OnError, and the handlers are installed. Calling it again while on is harmless. Off: the component stops receiving them; when it was the last one the file is closed. The handlers themselves stay installed - the test suite may own them, and with nobody subscribed they cost nothing until a critical fires.

parameters.name: owner
parameters.summary: The component; the subscription is keyed by it and holds it weakly.

parameters.name: report
parameters.summary: Raises the component's OnError with a message. It must be static - the component comes back as its first argument - or it would keep the component alive from this static list. The component's OnError is raised directly, not through its logger: an engine's inner pipeline replaces the logger on the context the two share, and outlives it.

parameters.name: logDirectory
parameters.summary: The component's Debug_Dir. The first subscriber opens the criticals file there, creating the directory; later subscribers share that file, and it stays where it was opened.

parameters.name: on
parameters.summary: True to subscribe, false to unsubscribe.

methods.name: ReportSetup
methods.summary: Reports a setup problem to the subscribed components - onlyOwner, or all of them - when it differs from the last one each was told about, and forgets it once it is gone. LoggerConfigure re-runs Boolean) on every Debug_* change, so an unchanged problem is said once and a new one - another unwritable Debug_Dir - is said again. Under its own prefix, so a handler counting "[NativeCritical]" counts criticals only; through String), outside every lock, so a throwing OnError never fails a setter or a Start.

methods.name: TryOpenFile
methods.summary: Opens the criticals file unless one is open. The directory and the file are created outside _sync: every thread that raises a critical takes that lock, and a Debug_Dir on an unreachable share would stall them for its timeout.
methods.returns: The failure to report, or null.

methods.name: InstallForSubscribers
methods.summary: Installs the handlers again once GStreamer is initialised: before that the native GLib may not have been loadable, and Suspend (DestroySDK) removed them for a teardown the SDK came back from. Tells the subscribers if they could not be installed.

methods.name: InstallIfWanted
methods.summary: Installs the handlers when anyone wants them: a subscribed component, or an Boolean) caller (the test suite) whose handlers DestroySDK removed.

methods.name: Suspend
methods.summary: Removes the handlers but keeps the subscriptions, the recording and the file. Called by DestroySDK: a host may unload its AppDomain after it (a .NET Framework plugin host, an IIS recycle) and must not leave GLib a callback into it. When the SDK comes back in the same domain, GstInitializer.Init installs them again through InstallForSubscribers.

methods.name: UpdateCaptureStacks
methods.summary: Stack capture is on while anyone asked for it: an Boolean) caller, or a subscriber, who is diagnosing a crash in the field and for whom the stack is the point. Caller holds _sync.

methods.name: PruneSubscribers
methods.summary: Drops the subscriptions whose component has been collected. Caller holds _sync.

methods.name: DetachIfUnsubscribed
methods.summary: Takes the file away once nobody is subscribed, for the caller to close after releasing _sync - closing waits for a write in progress. Caller holds _sync.
methods.returns: The file to close, or null.

methods.name: Reset
methods.summary: Clears the recorded criticals. Call it at the start of a test so the assertion at the end covers only that test.

methods.name: GetLifetimeCriticals
methods.summary: Gets the recorded criticals that mean the SDK mismanaged a native object's lifetime.
methods.remarks: All of these are a defect in the calling code rather than in GStreamer. The count has been wrong before — it said "four" while the list held five, and then six — so read the list, not the number, and update both together: GST_IS_* — a wrapper was used after its handle was zeroed.G_TYPE_CHECK_INSTANCE — the GLib spelling of the line above, and the same defect: a type check failing on a pointer that is no longer a valid GObject. GStreamer's own macros print a GST_IS_* name, but a plain GObject API prints the macro as written — g_signal_handlers_disconnect_matched: assertion 'G_TYPE_CHECK_INSTANCE (instance)' failed was recorded and then filtered straight back out for as long as only the GStreamer spelling was matched (bugs.md #51). The OTHER GLib spelling of a failed type check, G_IS_OBJECT, is deliberately NOT in this list: it is printed by g_object_set / _get / _ref / _unref / g_signal_connect and would arm an assembly-wide matcher over a far larger surface. The teardown-race tests that need it filter by hand, and that is the way to assert on it - do not remove those filters expecting this list to cover them.instance with invalid (NULL) class pointer — the FIRST line of that cascade, raised by g_type_check_instance itself (gtype.c) before the caller's assertion prints. It is a g_critical, not a g_warning, so it does clear ; and it names a freed instance more directly than the assertion that follows it.still has a parent — something dropped a reference it did not own.instead of the NULL state — an element was released before it was stopped.no signal watches attached — a bus watch was removed twice.ref_count > 0 — an object was unreffed once too often.REFCOUNT_VALUE — the mini-object half of the same defect. gst_mini_object_unref asserts GST_MINI_OBJECT_REFCOUNT_VALUE (mini_object) > 0 (gstminiobject.c), which the ref_count > 0 wording of gst_object_unref does not match — so an over-unreffed caps, buffer, event, message or sample used to scroll past unmatched. Every gst_<type>_unref is a static inline over this one, so the single fragment covers them all.priv->started — gst_device_monitor_dispose asserts !self->priv->started; disposing a started monitor leaves the provider's probe running.toggle ref outlived — raised by the managed binding, not by GLib: a queued ToggleRef release found its GObject already finalized. Native code cannot report this one, because by then there is nothing left to assert on — the unguarded call simply crashed the process instead (bug #50).VisioForge-Invariant: — raised by the SDK itself through , in Debug builds: user code reached while an SDK lock was held, the shape that deadlocks an error handler marshalling to a UI thread (issue #1711). The type-check assertion alone is NOT enough to protect this SDK: the encoder-factory over-unref and the dispose-while-PAUSED defect both raise one of the other shapes and would have gone on passing a suite that only looked for GST_IS_. ref_count > 0 earns its place by being the FIRST line of a cascade rather than the loudest. In a full run it appears once, immediately before the process-global GStreamer registry stops answering and a thousand GST_IS_REGISTRY criticals follow it. Matching only the loud ones fails a hundred innocent tests and names none of the culprits.
methods.returns: The matching messages; empty when there are none.

methods.name: IsKnownUpstreamNoise
methods.summary: True for the one critical this SDK knows to be upstream noise rather than a defect in the calling code: object MXFMetadata*/MXFDMS1* 0x… finalized while still in-construction.
methods.remarks: mxfdemux builds its metadata objects with the low-level GType allocator instead of g_object_new — ret = (MXFMetadata *) g_type_create_instance (t); in mxf_metadata_new and its mxf_descriptive_metadata_new twin (gst-plugins-bad, gst/mxf/mxfmetadata.c). That allocates the instance and runs instance_init, so the in-construction flag g_object_init sets is never cleared: only g_object_new_internal clears it, and the object never goes through it. GObject then criticals on every one of them from g_object_finalize (gobject.c). Nothing is wrong with the object. The flag governs two things — writing a CONSTRUCT_ONLY property and queueing rather than dispatching a notify — and the MXFMetadata* types carry no GObject properties at all, so neither branch is reachable. Finalize runs, memory is released, the file plays and the SDK reports the truth. It is filtered because of what it costs THIS type, not because it is untidy: one MXF file raises 513 of them (measured, macOS, MXF_MPEG2_PCM.mxf). That fills after eight files, and once the cap is reached a genuine critical is counted but not stored — reads the list, so the assembly guard would pass on a real defect. Recording known noise here would disarm the diagnostic this type exists to be. The complaint alone is not enough to match on. "finalized while still in-construction" by itself would silence the same GObject complaint from any other plugin — including one this SDK does own — and that has never been measured, so an MXF type name has to be there as well. Two name prefixes, because GObject prints the LEAF type name (G_OBJECT_TYPE_NAME (object)). mxf_metadata_new instantiates the MXFMetadata* types; its mxf_descriptive_metadata_new twin has the identical defect but instantiates the 32 MXFDMS1* types of mxfdms1.c, whose names carry no "MXFMetadata" at all. That second family raises nothing today only because mxf_element_init ships mxf_dms1_initialize () commented out (gstmxfelement.c:71), so no descriptive-metadata scheme is registered and the twin returns NULL before it allocates. Covering it here costs one fragment and does not depend on that line staying commented out. Upstream: freedesktop/gstreamer#3921, open since 2024 and still present on main; ours: GitHub issue #1273.

parameters.name: message
parameters.summary: The GLib message text, without the domain.

methods.returns: True when the message is the known mxfdemux noise.

methods.name: TakeSubscriberStack
methods.summary: Whether this critical may capture a stack for the subscribers; see MaxSubscriberStacksPerSecond.
methods.remarks: Lock-free: it runs on the raising thread for every critical, and a cascade is exactly when those threads must not queue on _sync. The count restarts every second, so it cannot run away; across a window boundary up to twice the rate can pass, which is fine for a throttle.

methods.name: Deliver
methods.summary: Hands a critical to the subscribed components: the file synchronously, each component's OnError on the thread pool. The handler runs on whatever thread raised the critical - often a GStreamer streaming thread - and an OnError handler that stops the pipeline from there would wait for its own thread to exit.

methods.name: Raise
methods.summary: Runs a component's report, catching what its OnError handler throws: on the thread pool that would take the process down - the opposite of what a crash diagnostic is for - and on a setter's thread it would fail a Debug_* setter or a Start over a diagnostics problem.

classes.name: Subscription

The component is held weakly - one that is never switched off must not be kept alive by this static list - and the report is a static method that gets the component back as its first argument, so it holds no reference of its own.

classes.name: LogDeferral
classes.summary: A region in which BaseContext holds back its logger writes and makes them when the outermost region on this thread is left. A logger can run customer code on the logging thread - a sink set through ILogger) - so a lock a customer thread can wait on is taken inside the region: using (LogDeferral.Enter()) lock (x) { ... }, and the writes run after the lock is released (issue #3650).

properties.name: IsActive
properties.summary: Gets whether this thread is inside a region.

methods.name: Enter
methods.summary: Enters a region; dispose the result to leave it.
methods.returns: The region to dispose.

methods.name: TryDefer
methods.summary: Holds a logger write back until the outermost region on this thread is left. The event is made now, so it carries the time and the trace of the log call, not of the release - and so it can reach a sink after an event another thread logged later.
methods.returns: false outside a region: the caller writes now.

classes.name: HeldWrite
classes.summary: A write held back: the event made at the log call, or - for a logger that does not bind templates - what the direct path writes.

classes.name: NoUserCodeScope
classes.summary: A region in which the SDK holds a lock that a customer thread can be waiting on, so nothing inside it may reach customer code - and every SDK log call can, through the logger's OnError sink (issue #1711).
classes.remarks: Debug builds count the regions per thread, and BaseContext reports a log call made inside one through String), which fails the test that made it. Release builds count nothing. Used as lock (x) using (NoUserCodeScope.Enter()) { ... }.

properties.name: IsInside
properties.summary: Gets whether this thread is inside a region. Always false in Release builds.

methods.name: Enter
methods.summary: Enters a region; dispose the result to leave it.
methods.returns: The scope to dispose.

classes.name: DSPConverter
classes.summary: Static methods to convert between different sample formats.
classes.remarks: Code is mainly based on information available on the original C source code pa_converters.c from Portable Audio I/O Library. This class try to be as fast as possible without using unsafe code. Dither isn't currently supported. Currently supported conversions are 'to' and 'from' conversions between the following value types: Integer 8-bit (byte), Integer 16-bit (Int16), Integer 32-bit (Int32), Single precision 32-bit floating point (float). Which are the most common PCM formats. To use it, just call Convert. The compiler will automatically detect which method to call based on your data types. Couldn't be simplier. int[] srcPcm16samples = new int[] { 1, 2, 3}; float[] destIeeeFloat32samples = new float[3]; SampleConverter.Convert(srcPcm16samples, destIeeeFloat32samples); // destIeeeFloat32samples now contains the converted samples.
