methods.summary: Sets the pipeline context that contains shared resources and configuration for the entire MediaBlocks pipeline. This context provides access to GStreamer objects, logging, licensing information, and other pipeline-wide resources.

parameters.name: context
parameters.summary: The BlockPipelineContext instance to associate with this block.

methods.name: SetPipeline
methods.summary: Associates this media block with a specific MediaBlocks pipeline and initializes the pipeline context. This method is typically called automatically when the block is added to a pipeline.

parameters.name: pipeline
parameters.summary: The MediaBlocksPipeline instance that will own this block.

methods.name: ResetBuildState
methods.summary: Clears the built latch so the next Build call recreates this block's elements. Called by the pipeline right after CleanUp() when a stopped pipeline is kept alive for a restart. A block whose latch survived its cleanup short-circuits Build to success while owning no elements at all — it silently contributes nothing to the rebuilt graph.
methods.remarks: THIS is the authoritative reset. The pipeline calls it for every block it owns, so a block author does not have to know the rule for the restart path to work. Individual blocks also clear _isBuilt at the top of their own CleanUp(). That is deliberate redundancy, not a second mechanism: assigning false twice costs nothing, and it keeps blocks correct on the paths the pipeline does not drive — a block cleaned up directly, or a child of a super block that was never connected and so never entered the pipeline's list. If the two ever disagree, this method is the one that decides.

methods.name: Build
methods.summary: Builds and initializes this media block, creating any necessary GStreamer elements and configuring them. This method must be overridden in derived classes to implement block-specific initialization logic.
methods.returns: true if the block was successfully built; otherwise, false.

methods.name: CreateElements
methods.summary: Creates the internal GStreamer elements used by this media block. Override this method in derived classes that need to create GStreamer elements. This method is typically called from the Build() method.
methods.returns: true if elements were successfully created; otherwise, false.

methods.name: AddElementsToPipeline
methods.summary: Adds the GStreamer elements owned by this block to the pipeline. Override this method in derived classes that manage GStreamer elements. This method is called automatically when the block is added to a pipeline.

methods.name: RemoveElementsFromPipeline
methods.summary: Removes the GStreamer elements owned by this block from the running pipeline. Disconnect the block's pads first (for example with DisconnectLive).
methods.remarks: By default this takes out every element a pad walk places inside the block - from its input pads (Inputs / Outputs, or Input / Output for a block implementing only those) through its main elements to its output pads, or, for a block with no outputs, to its sink or up to another block's input - in which case the removal is refused, so remove such a block before taking the block it feeds out of the pipeline - without linking its neighbours to each other, then releases them and resets IsBuilt; dispose the block afterwards. The block's inputs must be disconnected; its single output may still be linked, and the block downstream is left as it is. All or nothing: a source, a block the walk cannot account for in full (one with no single chain of elements - most outputs, effects and composite blocks), a block with several outputs, or one whose input is still connected is left untouched and a warning is logged. The exception is an RTSPServerBlock, whose video and audio inputs are removed one chain at a time: if a chain cannot be removed, an error is logged, a chain already removed stays out of the pipeline, and the block stays built; calling this again removes the rest. The pipeline's own stop does not rely on it. GitHub issue #2139.

methods.name: DeepCopy
methods.summary: Creates and returns a deep copy of this media block with a new unique name. The clone will have the same configuration but will be a separate instance. Override this method in derived classes to implement block-specific cloning logic.

parameters.name: newName
parameters.summary: The name to assign to the cloned block. If null or empty, a name will be auto-generated.

methods.returns: A new instance of the media block with the same configuration as the original.

methods.name: Reset
methods.summary: Resets this media block to its initial state, clearing any accumulated data or state. Override this method in derived classes that maintain internal state that needs to be reset.

methods.name: ClearPads
methods.summary: Clears all input and output pad references for this media block. This method is typically called during cleanup or disposal to ensure proper resource release.

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Releases unmanaged and - optionally - managed resources. Override this method in derived classes to implement block-specific cleanup logic.
methods.remarks: An override must call its CleanUp() only under disposing. Finalize reaches this method with false, and a block's CleanUp() releases GstSharp wrappers - which takes GStreamer locks and can block - on the finalizer thread, which must never do either. A block that is never disposed leaves its elements to the pipeline that owns them; that is what their toggle refs are for. base.Dispose(disposing) stays outside the guard, because the latch below has to be set on both paths. The one carve-out is a block holding a resource nothing else can release - a device handle, say, which no pipeline owns and no toggle ref reclaims; such a block may run its CleanUp() on the finalizer path, guarded against throwing, and has to say why at the call site (see AndroidUVCSourceBlock). GitHub issue #958.

parameters.name: disposing
parameters.summary: true to release both managed and unmanaged resources; false to release only unmanaged resources.

methods.name: Finalize
methods.summary: Finalizes an instance of the MediaBlock class.

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Performs application-defined tasks associated with freeing, releasing, or resetting unmanaged resources.

methods.name: ReleasePads
methods.summary: Disconnects (optionally) and disposes every pad a block owns.
methods.remarks: Dispose removes the EOS probe that SetInternalPad installs unconditionally; that probe's GCHandle is a GC root holding the pad, and the pad holds its Block, so an undisposed pad pins the whole block graph for the life of the process. GitHub issue #827. Best called while the elements owning the static pads are still alive, but it does not depend on it: does not dispose its Gst.Pad wrapper, and that wrapper holds the transfer-full reference gst_element_get_static_pad handed it - so the pad outlives the element that parented it and gst_pad_remove_probe still sees a valid GST_IS_PAD. Only pads the block actually owns are released: SuperMediaBlock proxies its children's pads through /, and those are the child's to release. Disposal is idempotent, so a block that also releases its own pads is unaffected.

parameters.name: block
parameters.summary: The block whose pads are released.

parameters.name: disconnect

classes.name: MediaBlockPad
classes.summary: Represents a connection point (pad) on a MediaBlock that enables data flow between blocks in the pipeline. Pads can be input (sink) or output (source) and are typed by media content (video, audio, subtitles, data). This class manages the underlying GStreamer pad, connection state, and provides methods for dynamic linking/unlinking during pipeline execution. Essential for building flexible media processing workflows.

constructors.name: MediaBlockPad
constructors.summary: Initializes a new instance of the MediaBlockPad class with the specified parameters. Creates a connection point for the given block with the specified data flow direction and media type.

parameters.name: block
parameters.summary: The MediaBlock that owns this pad.

parameters.name: direction
parameters.summary: The data flow direction (input/sink or output/source).

parameters.name: mediaType
parameters.summary: The type of media content this pad will handle (video, audio, subtitles, data).

parameters.name: onDemandConnect
parameters.summary: If true, the pad will connect dynamically after pipeline start; if false, connects during pipeline construction.

properties.name: Direction

properties.summary: Gets the type of media content that flows through this pad (video, audio, subtitles, or data). This determines what kind of media streams can be connected to this pad.
properties.value: The media type specifying the kind of content this pad handles.

properties.summary: Gets or sets a value indicating whether this pad will establish its connection dynamically after the pipeline starts. When true, the pad connection is deferred until runtime rather than being established during pipeline construction.
properties.value: True if the pad connects on-demand after pipeline start; otherwise, false for immediate connection.

properties.summary: Gets or sets a custom tag object that can be used to associate additional data with this pad. This is typically used for internal bookkeeping or storing pad-specific metadata.

properties.name: IsDropGuarded
properties.summary: Whether the output's pad carries the drop probe now.

methods.name: SetInternalPad
methods.summary: Associates this MediaBlockPad with the underlying GStreamer pad object. This establishes the connection between the high-level MediaBlocks pad and the low-level GStreamer pad.

parameters.name: pad
parameters.summary: The GStreamer pad object that will handle the actual media data flow.

methods.name: IsOnDemandConnection
methods.summary: Whether the build leaves this pad unlinked for a later ConnectLive: it, or the pad it is connected to, is flagged OnDemandConnect.
methods.returns: true for an on-demand connection.

methods.name: LeaveOutOfBuild
methods.summary: Leaves this input out of a muxer's or mixer's build when the connection that fed it was dropped (_forgottenLive) and nothing connected it since, while another input of the block is connected, on a start (not a live add). The element waits for data on every pad it hands out, so a pad for this input would hold the restart forever (issue #3976); the output is written with the inputs that are fed. The pad the previous build gave this input is dropped, so a later ConnectLive into it fails instead of linking into a released element. An input never connected keeps its pad, for a ConnectLive after the start.

parameters.name: pipeline
parameters.summary: The pipeline the block builds into.

methods.returns: true when the build is to request no pad for this input.

methods.name: IsLiveBuild
methods.summary: Whether a build adds a block to a pipeline already out of NULL or changing state - a live add, which has no connection to read yet: ConnectLive needs the pads the build creates. A start builds in NULL (#3734).

parameters.name: pipeline
parameters.summary: The pipeline the block builds into.

methods.returns: true for a live add.

methods.name: DropWhileUnlinked
methods.summary: Drops the data at an on-demand output's GStreamer pad, at any output MediaBlockPad) unlinks, at an active (PAUSED or PLAYING) output Disconnect unlinks, and at any output linked with MediaBlockPad) or added by TeeBlock.AddNewPadLive, and at an output that lost its input (LostItsInput, #3948), while the pad has no peer. The queue behind it would otherwise push into nothing and get not-linked, which reaches the source's shared streaming thread and keeps the pipeline out of PLAYING or fails the source (issues #1799, #2056, #2132). It also drops while the peer is still flushing: a consumer linked live is in NULL until it is synced, and a push into it returns FLUSHING, which a queue keeps for good and a tee hands upstream, stopping every output (#3409). A dropped sticky event stays pending and goes ahead of the first buffer that passes (gstpad.c, push_sticky); a dropped non-sticky event is lost, as it would be with no peer. EOS is never dropped. The probe stays while the pad is the output's, so an unlink later on is covered too; a buffer already past the probe when MediaBlockPad) or Disconnect unlinks the pad is covered by Pad). It goes when the output moves to another pad (Pad)) and in Dispose. A linked output carrying it pays one managed call per buffer for it.

parameters.name: anyOutput
parameters.summary: Arms the probe on any output, not only an on-demand one: the pad is about to be unlinked, or about to be linked live.

methods.name: UnlinkGuarded
methods.summary: Unlinks this output so that a buffer in flight does not come back not-linked (#3716). gst_pad_push_data runs a probe without the pad's lock and reads the peer after it, so a buffer PadProbeInfo) let through can find the peer gone. Adding a probe changes the pad's probe list cookie, and that push then calls the new probe before it reads the peer (do_probe_callbacks). Removing one does not change the cookie, so the barrier cannot simply come off after the unlink: the output's own probe is replaced first, with one that push has not called yet and that now sees no peer.
methods.remarks: An IDLE probe would not do: the pad counts as in use only after the peer read, so one fires while the push is still in the window. One gap stays open: a sticky event still pending after the push's last probe pass (stored on the pad during the push, or dropped by this probe at a flushing peer) makes it drop the lock once more before it reads the peer (check_sticky). This rests on gstpad.c internals, which the test MP4SinkBlock_DisconnectLive_BufferPastTheDropProbe pins for each redist.

parameters.name: inPad
parameters.summary: The pad it is linked to.

methods.returns: What gst_pad_unlink returned.

methods.name: ArmDropAhead
methods.summary: Arms the drop probe ahead on next, the pad a live edit is about to make this output's, while that pad still has its peer: the edit then unlinks a pad that already drops. Only for an output that is guarded now. Pad) adopts the probe; CancelPendingDrop removes it when the output does not move there.

parameters.name: next
parameters.summary: The pad the output is about to move to.

methods.name: CancelPendingDrop
methods.summary: Removes a drop probe armed ahead (Pad)) that the output did not move to.

methods.name: LeaveDropProbe
methods.summary: Removes the drop probe of the pad the output leaves for next, and a probe armed ahead for any other pad. A null next is teardown. The caller holds _dropLock.

parameters.name: next
parameters.summary: The pad the output moves to, or null.

methods.name: RemoveNextDropProbe
methods.summary: Removes the probe armed ahead. The caller holds _dropLock.

methods.name: RemoveDropProbe
methods.summary: Removes a drop probe, logging rather than throwing.

methods.name: DropUnlinked
methods.summary: Drops data that has no peer to go to, or whose peer is not active yet.
methods.remarks: The peer is read raw rather than through Peer: that returns the one cached wrapper of the peer pad, which another holder may have disposed, and this runs on a streaming thread.

methods.name: DropAllButEos
methods.summary: Drops everything but EOS: Pad)'s barrier, and what PadProbeInfo) does once it has decided to drop.

methods.name: AddEOSHandler
methods.summary: Adds an End-of-Stream (EOS) event handler to the underlying GStreamer pad. This enables detection of when media processing completes on this pad.

methods.name: RetainCallback
methods.summary: Holds a probe delegate alive past the removal of its probe, keeping one generation of slack.
methods.remarks: The pad object now survives a pipeline stop, so retaining every delegate this pad ever installed — the old behaviour — grew this list by one per restart cycle and only ever emptied it in Dispose. Unlike the pad wrapper itself, nothing reclaims these: it is a plain managed list, so a long-running recorder accumulated one delegate per pad per cycle for the life of the process. Two entries keep the delegate whose probe was just removed and the one before it, which is strictly more slack than the hazard needs — that hazard is an in-flight probe racing its own RemoveProbe, resolved within the same swap, not two swaps later.

methods.name: ProbeCallbackCall
methods.summary: Callback method that monitors events flowing through the GStreamer pad. Watches for End-of-Stream (EOS) events and triggers the appropriate handlers, and for a mid-stream video frame size change on a recording branch (see Event)).

parameters.name: pad
parameters.summary: The GStreamer pad that triggered the probe.

parameters.name: info
parameters.summary: Information about the probe event, including event type and data.

methods.returns: PadProbeReturn.Ok to continue normal processing of the event, or PadProbeReturn.Drop for a caps event that would change the frame size under a muxer that cannot take one.

methods.name: ResetNegotiatedFrameSize
methods.summary: Forgets the frame size remembered from the caps events seen so far.
methods.remarks: Called from Pad) only. A downstream STREAM_START deliberately does NOT reset it: the muxer this guard protects did not restart with the upstream stream, its track header is already written, and a new stream arriving at a live recording branch at a different size - what input-selector delivers when SourceSwitchBlock switches sources mid-take - is precisely the condition to report, not to forget.

methods.name: ReportError
methods.summary: Logs an error off the streaming thread.
methods.remarks: Context.Error reaches the application's OnError synchronously through the Serilog observable sink, and everything here runs inside a pad probe on the streaming thread with the pad's stream lock held. A handler that reacts by stopping the pipeline - which is exactly what the frame-size message asks for - would then be waiting on the thread it is running on. Deferring the raise is what makes that instruction safe to follow; Bus_Error defers its own state change for the same reason. The price is ordering: the raise is queued before the EOS is injected but may be delivered after the branch has already stopped, so an application must not treat "no error yet" at the moment of the stop as "the recording ended cleanly".

parameters.name: method
parameters.summary: The reporting member, for the log line.

methods.name: CheckFrameSizeChange
methods.summary: Detects a mid-stream video frame size change on an input pad feeding a muxer that cannot take one, reports it as an error and finalizes that branch.
methods.remarks: Issue #1496. A caps change reaching a live recording branch - a device rotation makes videoflip swap width and height, but anything that renegotiates gets here - used to produce a single GStreamer WARNING from gst_video_filter_transform and nothing else: the recording carried on and wrote an undecodable H.264 tail while nothing reached OnError and StopAsync completed normally. The caps event is serialized ahead of the first buffer of the new size, so this is the last moment at which nothing is corrupt yet. The EOS and the Drop belong together. Dropping the caps event alone would leave the downstream videoconvert negotiated for the old size while buffers of the new one arrive - and NV12 720x1280 and 1280x720 are the same number of bytes, so nothing notices and the file fills with transposed rows. The EOS puts the pad in EOS instead, so the next gst_pad_chain answers GST_FLOW_EOS and the branch stops without a second noisy message. The EOS goes to this pad only, never to the block's other pads: a sibling audio pad's stream lock is held by the audio thread sitting inside the muxer's aggregator, and taking it from here is a deadlock. In an A/V recording the video track therefore stops here while the moov is written by the normal StopAsync - which the error message asks for. Sending the event from inside this pad's own probe is safe: GST_PAD_STREAM_LOCK is a recursive mutex, so the nested take by the same thread passes, and the probe callback runs with GST_OBJECT_LOCK released. DynamicPipeline does the same from a blocking probe. The injected EOS does run this pad's probes again, so fires nested inside this call - on the same streaming thread a naturally arriving EOS would have fired it on, which is why no subscriber needs to care; the once-only flag is what keeps this member itself out of the recursion.

parameters.name: pad
parameters.summary: The pad the caps event arrived on.

methods.returns: true when the caps event must be dropped.

methods.summary: Gets the underlying GStreamer pad object associated with this MediaBlockPad. Provides access to the low-level GStreamer pad for advanced operations.
methods.returns: The GStreamer Pad object, or null if not yet assigned.

methods.name: Connect
methods.summary: Establishes a logical connection between this pad and another MediaBlockPad. This creates a high-level connection relationship that will be used for pipeline construction.

parameters.name: pad
parameters.summary: The target MediaBlockPad to connect to.

methods.name: GetConnectedToPad
methods.summary: Gets the MediaBlockPad that this pad is currently connected to. Returns the logical connection established through the Connect method or ConnectLive.
methods.returns: The connected MediaBlockPad, or null if not connected.

methods.name: IsConnected
methods.summary: Determines whether this pad has a logical connection to another MediaBlockPad. This checks the high-level connection established through the Connect method or ConnectLive.
methods.returns: True if this pad is connected to another MediaBlockPad; otherwise, false.

methods.name: LostItsInput
methods.summary: Whether this output lost the input it fed and nothing connected it since (#3948).
methods.returns: true for such an output.

methods.name: IsConsumed
methods.summary: Whether anything downstream takes this output's data: it is connected, flagged to connect after the pipeline starts, or its GStreamer pad is already linked (a raw link records no connection).
methods.remarks: A decoder block leaves the decoded pad of an unconsumed output unlinked, which the decoder tolerates while another of its streams is linked. Fed into the block's own queue instead, it pushes into a pad with no peer, and after a seek the queue fails the next EOS with not-linked (issue #1702). Read once, when the decoded pad appears: an output linked live after that is not fed.
methods.returns: true if the output is consumed.

methods.name: Disconnect
methods.summary: Disconnects this pad from its currently connected MediaBlockPad. This performs actual GStreamer pad unlinking and clears the logical connection on both sides. On a paused or playing pipeline the output then drops its data until it is linked again, and the sinks it fed stop counting for a pause, a seek or the end of stream until data reaches them again (#3936). A push already inside the cut branch is let out first, so the call may wait for it - up to two seconds. A restart leaves the input out as after MediaBlockPad), and the output, unless it is connected again, drops its data with a warning instead of failing the start (#3948).

methods.name: IsConnectedLive
methods.summary: Determines whether the underlying GStreamer pad is actively linked in a running pipeline. This checks the actual GStreamer-level connection status, not just the logical MediaBlocks connection.
methods.returns: True if the GStreamer pad is actively linked; otherwise, false.

methods.name: ConnectLive
methods.summary: Dynamically links this source pad to a sink pad in a running or paused pipeline. This allows for runtime connection changes without stopping the pipeline. Called on a sink pad, it links sinkPad to it instead, as MediaBlockPad) does. The link is recorded as a connection, so a stop and start of the pipeline links the pads again - unless either pad has OnDemandConnect, which leaves the link to the caller after every start.

parameters.name: sinkPad
parameters.summary: The target sink MediaBlockPad to link to, or the source pad when this is a sink pad.

methods.returns: True if the pads were linked, or the output is already linked to the input; false if linking failed, including when the output is linked to another pad.

methods.name: ConnectLive
methods.summary: MediaBlockPad), reporting through context: MediaBlocksPipeline.ConnectLive passes its own.

methods.name: RecordConnection
methods.summary: Records a live link as a connection, as Connect does, so a stop and start relinks it (#3749). Not for an on-demand pair: a build leaves it for the caller to link after each start, and a record would have a block such as the NDI sink build a branch nobody feeds.

parameters.name: input
parameters.summary: The input this output is linked to.

methods.name: ForgetLiveConnection
methods.summary: Forgets the connection to pad when MediaBlockPad) recorded it (#3749).

methods.name: ForgetConnectionTo
methods.summary: Forgets the connection to a pad of block, however it was made (#3749).

methods.summary: ForgetConnection for a pad whose connection is cut, on either side: this pad is marked too, not only the other one.

methods.name: ForgetConnection
methods.summary: Clears this pad's connection, and the other pad's when it points back here.

methods.name: IsParked
methods.summary: Whether this output was left unconnected at build time and parked on a null sink by its pipeline.

methods.name: ParkedConnectError
methods.summary: The ConnectLive refusal of a parked output, with how to keep it connectable.

methods.name: DisconnectLive
methods.summary: Dynamically unlinks this source pad from a sink pad in a running or paused pipeline. This allows for runtime disconnection without stopping the pipeline. Called on a sink pad, it unlinks sinkPad from it instead. A connection MediaBlockPad) recorded is forgotten, so a stop and start leaves the pads unlinked; one made with Connect stays, and the start links it again. When the forgotten connection fed a muxing output or sink, or an AudioMixerBlock, that keeps another input connected, the block is rebuilt without that input and writes only the connected tracks; that input then takes no ConnectLive, on this start or any later one, until it is connected again with Connect while the pipeline is stopped (#3976). A multivariant HLSSinkBlock cannot drop a variant or rendition, and refuses the start instead. A block left in the pipeline with no input connected is rebuilt with nothing feeding it on a restart; its sinks do not hold the start, and a ConnectLive into it brings them back (#3936). The sinks the input fed stop counting in the running pipeline too: a pause, a seek or the end of stream does not wait for them until data reaches them again. A push already inside the cut branch is let out first, so the call may wait for it - up to two seconds.

parameters.name: sinkPad
parameters.summary: The sink MediaBlockPad to unlink from, or the source pad when this is a sink pad.

methods.returns: True if the pads were successfully unlinked; false if unlinking failed.

methods.summary: Unblocks data flow through this pad in a running pipeline. This resumes media data flow through a previously blocked pad.
methods.returns: True if the pad is unblocked when this returns, including when it was never blocked. One call lifts the block however many times BlockPadLive was called.

classes.name: MediaBlocksPipeline
classes.summary: The modern, cross-platform MediaBlocks pipeline implementation for building flexible media processing workflows. This class is the core orchestrator that manages media blocks (sources, effects, encoders, sinks), controls their lifecycle, and handles data flow between blocks through the underlying multimedia framework. It provides a high-level API for creating complex media applications including video players, recorders, transcoders, and streaming solutions across Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android platforms.
classes.remarks: The MediaBlocksPipeline serves as the container and coordinator for media blocks. Key responsibilities include: - Managing the collection of media blocks and their connections - Building and initializing the media pipeline infrastructure - Controlling pipeline state (Free, Playing, Paused) - Processing bus messages and translating them to .NET events - Handling errors and providing diagnostic information - Managing resource cleanup and disposal This is the foundation class for the MediaBlocks SDK, which represents the most flexible and powerful approach to media processing in the VisioForge Media Framework.

constructors.name: MediaBlocksPipeline
constructors.summary: Initializes a new instance of the MediaBlocksPipeline class with optional name and logging context. This constructor creates a new pipeline instance ready to accept media blocks and build processing workflows.
constructors.remarks: The constructor performs essential initialization: - Loads the multimedia framework libraries and initializes the system - Sets up logging infrastructure (Serilog) - Configures local library redistribution paths (Windows only) - Creates the internal media pipeline object - Sets up error handling callbacks After construction, add media blocks using AddBlock() and connect them before calling Build() and Start().

methods.name: TryEnterBusCallback
methods.summary: Marks the calling bus callback as in flight, unless teardown has already begun.
methods.remarks: Increment-then-recheck is deliberate and pairs with Bus), which writes the flag and then reads the counter. Interlocked.Increment is a full fence, so at least one of the two threads observes the other: either teardown sees a non-zero count and waits for this callback, or this callback sees the flag and bails out. Neither side can slip through.

parameters.name: asyncDispatch

methods.name: DisposePipelineWhenBusIsIdle
methods.summary: Releases a pipeline that must not be freed on the calling thread, from the GLib main loop that owns the bus dispatch, once that dispatch has provably unwound.
methods.remarks: Waiting for _busCallbacksInFlight to reach zero would NOT be enough, and that is the whole reason this goes through an idle source. The counter is decremented by in the managed handler's finally, so zero means "the managed body returned", not "the native gst_bus_source_dispatch frame finished" — and the frame goes on using the bus after the handler returns. Worse, the waiter is woken by the PulseAll inside that same finally, so it would free the pipeline at the earliest and most dangerous instant of the window rather than a random later one. That is the defect which hung the macOS suite 3 runs out of 3, re-armed with a lock handoff of jitter instead of none. A main-context source carries the guarantee the counter cannot express. GstInitializer runs a GLib.MainLoop on MainContext.Default, gst_bus_add_signal_watch attaches the bus watch to that same default context, and a GMainContext dispatches its sources one at a time on one thread. So this callback cannot run while the ASYNC dispatch that caused the deferral is still on that thread's stack — not as a race won, but by construction. It covers only the async half, which is why the counter check is still here. Bus_SyncMessage is emitted by gst_bus_post on whichever STREAMING thread posted the message, so it is counted in _busCallbacksInFlight but is not serialised by this main context at all. A stop deferred because a sync handler was still in flight would otherwise be disposed on the very first dispatch, straight back into the use-after-free. Neither condition implies the other, so this re-arms on a short timer until both hold: the source proves the async dispatch unwound, the counter proves no handler of either kind is inside. A timer rather than an idle for exactly that reason — an idle handler that returns true is re-dispatched as fast as the loop can spin, so a wedged sync handler would turn a 10-second grace period into 10 seconds of a busy main loop. Disposing explicitly also keeps the release off the finalizer, which matters more than it looks: GLib.Object.Dispose(true) calls ToggleRef.Dispose() synchronously, while the finalizer path calls QueueUnref() — the ThreadPool-dispatched g_object_remove_toggle_ref that produced 0xC0000005 on Windows and is bugs.md #50. Dropping the reference instead of disposing would have routed every deferred teardown through exactly that site. If the main loop is already gone — process shutdown, VisioForgeX.StopMainLoop — the callback never runs and the wrapper stays alive to the end of the process. That is a bounded leak on a shutdown path, and strictly better than freeing memory a live frame is walking.

parameters.name: doomed
parameters.summary: The pipeline to release. May be null, in which case nothing happens.

methods.name: DetachBusAndWaitForCallbacks
methods.summary: Stops bus delivery and waits, bounded, for any callback already executing to leave.
methods.remarks: MUST be called before anything releases the native pipeline. The bus callbacks dereference the pipeline's NATIVE handle, and GLib.Object.Dispose frees the object synchronously on the calling thread — so without this barrier a callback could be inside gst_element_get_bus (which takes the object's own GMutex) while teardown destroys that mutex. That aborted the process with "pthread_mutex_unlock: Invalid argument" roughly one run in three. Neither gst_bus_remove_signal_watch nor detaching a signal handler waits for an emission already in progress, which is why the counter exists. This cannot deadlock. The bus thread never blocks here — it only touches interlocked counters and takes for the duration of a PulseAll. The stopping thread waits with a timeout and proceeds regardless. Call it AFTER the graceful-EOS wait in PerformStop: detaching earlier would stop Bus_EOS from ever setting the flag that wait keys off, spinning the full stop budget and truncating muxers.

parameters.name: bus
parameters.summary: The bus to detach the handlers from. May be null.

methods.returns: true when the caller must NOT free the native pipeline on this thread, for either of two reasons: the wait gave up with another thread's callback still running, or the stop was issued from inside one of this pipeline's own bus callbacks. The caller then hands the object to Pipeline), which still releases it with an explicit Dispose — just from the GLib main loop, once the dispatch has unwound. The second reason is not a weaker version of the first, it is a certainty rather than a race. A managed bus handler runs inside a live gst_bus_source_dispatch frame (confirmed by stack sample), and that native frame keeps using the bus after the handler returns. Excluding the caller's own frames from the WAIT is correct and is what removes the stall; concluding from that that the object is safe to FREE is not, and those two decisions have to stay separate.

Return true to suppress default handling, false to allow it.

A drain marks the run _videoDrained here already; the failed source is still recorded by Bus_Error and PopPendingErrors.

The snapshot itself is taken through GetSpecialBlocksSnapshot for the reason given in Bus_ParseLevel - direct enumeration races AddBlock / ClearBlocks.

The dispatch loop's IsBuilt check catches that once it has settled; this catches the dispose that lands between the check and the read. Kept apart from the catch around the delivery itself only so the two report what actually failed - a dispose the pipeline caused, or the application's own event handler. Both are per block: at the handler level either would abandon the rest of the snapshot and silence every meter behind this one (issue #1473).
