methods.name: StopAsync
methods.summary: Asynchronously stops the media pipeline and halts all processing operations without blocking the calling thread. This is the recommended method for stopping from UI threads to maintain responsiveness.

parameters.name: force
parameters.summary: If set to true, forces immediate pipeline shutdown without waiting for graceful EOS (End-of-Stream) processing. For file outputs, this may cause incomplete frames or file corruption. Use graceful shutdown (false) for production recording scenarios to ensure proper file finalization.

methods.returns: A Task that completes with a boolean value: true if stop was successful, false if already stopped.

methods.name: Stop
methods.summary: Stops the media pipeline and halts all processing operations. This method brings the pipeline to a complete stop and transitions to the Free state. Source blocks are stopped first, followed by pipeline state transition and resource cleanup.
methods.remarks: This method is thread-safe. Concurrent calls are serialized via _stopLock; only the first caller executes the stop sequence, subsequent calls return false.

parameters.name: force
parameters.summary: If set to true, forces immediate pipeline shutdown without waiting for graceful EOS processing. For file outputs, this may cause incomplete frames or file corruption. Use graceful shutdown (false) for production recording scenarios.

methods.returns: true if the pipeline was successfully stopped; false if the operation failed or stop was already in progress.

methods.name: TearDownGraph
methods.summary: The last part of a stop: takes the pipeline to NULL, detaches the bus and releases the GStreamer side through Boolean). Call it under _stopLock.

parameters.name: forRestart
parameters.summary: true to keep the block objects and the pad graph so the instance can be started again; false on disposal.

methods.name: PerformStop
methods.summary: Core stop sequence shared by the public Boolean) API and the natural End-Of-Stream teardown (Bus_EOS). Performs the full pipeline cleanup (stops sources, brings the pipeline to NULL, removes the bus signal watch, clears resources), resets the lifecycle latches, transitions to Free, and fires OnStop exactly once. Routing both paths through this method guarantees that a file reaching its end leaves the pipeline in the identical cleaned-up state as an explicit stop, so a subsequent StartAsync is never rejected with the misleading "Already starting" message.

parameters.name: force
parameters.summary: If set to true, forces immediate shutdown without injecting an EOS to flush muxers. Use graceful shutdown (false) for production recording scenarios.

parameters.name: stopPosition
parameters.summary: Position to report in OnStop. When null on a graceful stop the current pipeline position is queried so resume/progress consumers still receive a meaningful value; the EOS path passes the end position it already captured.

parameters.name: raiseStopEvent
parameters.summary: Set to false for an internal teardown that is not the end of a play cycle - a start that failed before it ever started. The event is then neither raised nor claimed, so a later real stop still gets its own OnStop.

methods.returns: true if the pipeline was stopped (or already stopped); false if another stop is in progress.

methods.name: OnlyRenderersEnd
methods.summary: Whether every block that ends a branch is a renderer, synced to the clock or not, and nothing handles a pad's OnEOS (issue #4062). Anything else that ends one - a file, a .NET stream, a network output, a custom or bridge sink - may still need the EOS to arrive, and so does an OnEOS handler (a TSAnalyzerBlock's final report, say): a graph holding one keeps the graceful wait. A sink hidden inside a block that has output pads is seen only when it writes a file.
methods.returns: true when there is at least one renderer, every end is one, no pad has an OnEOS handler, and no leaf sink of the built graph writes a file.

methods.name: DropRendererBuffers
methods.summary: Drops every buffer that reaches a renderer's input, or its sink's own pad, from now on, so no renderer paces the graph: the media queued ahead of the stop's End-Of-Stream drains at once into the outputs that need it (issue #4072). Events pass, so each renderer still gets its EOS and the graceful wait ends as before. Only while the pipeline is settled in PLAYING: a renderer that has to preroll - on the resume of a parked graph, a start still in flight, a flushing seek - gets its buffer, or the graph could never reach PLAYING for the EOS.

parameters.name: drops
parameters.summary: Receives each pad and probe id as it is installed, so a throw part way leaves none unowned.

methods.name: LeafSinkPad
methods.summary: Follows a renderer's input downstream to its sink's own pad, past a queue inside the renderer (the audio renderer holds 500 ms ahead of its sink). Stops at an element with no static src pad - the sink, a bin, a tee - and answers the pad it reached.

parameters.name: pad
parameters.summary: The renderer block's internal input pad, or null.

methods.returns: The pad to drop buffers on, or null.

methods.name: RemoveRendererDrops
methods.summary: Removes the probes UInt64}}) installed, once each. Never throws: it runs in the stop's finally too.

methods.name: ResetStartedFlag
methods.summary: Clears the started latch (_started). Deliberately NOT _starting: that one belongs to the Boolean) / Boolean) call that claimed it and is cleared by StartIntl's finally, or by the StartAsync catch when the pool never ran StartIntl. StartIntl performs its own teardown on its failure exits (the fatal-licence Stop(true), the failed build's TearDownGraph and the refused Pause/Play PerformStop), and a teardown that cleared the starting latch would drop the claim of the very start that called it - and, for a stop racing an unrelated start, the claim of a start it knows nothing about.

methods.name: InjectGracefulEos
methods.summary: Injects End-Of-Stream for a graceful stop: Element.SendEvent(EOS) on each source, the walk gst_bin_send_event would do, so live GstBaseSrc unlocks. Never through the pipeline: gst_element_send_event on it holds the pipeline's state lock, which the bin needs to commit a pending PLAYING (gstbin.c gst_bin_continue_func), while a source's streaming thread waits in a sink's preroll holding the stream lock the EOS needs - after EOS went into branches no stream reached (issue #1798), or a source with no queue at its output stopped right after its first frame (#2979). After a real bus error the failed source is skipped — forwarding EOS into it AVs (issue #825) — and EOS is pushed on the peer of each of its linked src pads instead, so muxers on that branch still get a trailer. A source whose streaming thread a muxer may hold for good (issue #4019) gets its EOS the same way, from a thread of its own.

parameters.name: pipeline
parameters.summary: The native pipeline. Caller has already null-checked it.

parameters.name: heldSources
parameters.summary: The sources such a muxer may hold (Boolean)); null for every source.

parameters.name: sends
parameters.summary: Where each send past a held source is added with the pad it goes to, or null.

methods.name: TryInjectGracefulEos
methods.summary: Thread}}) without the warning, for SendEOS, which reports it after its pipeline use ends (issue #1899).
methods.returns: false if the walk over the sources did not reach every source.

methods.name: LeaveOutOutputsOfHeldSources
methods.summary: Waits up to two seconds for the EOS sends past held sources, and adds the sinks behind every pad whose send still waits to leftOut: a streaming thread holds the stream lock that EOS needs, so none of the outputs behind that pad gets one, and the stop's wait must not hold out for them (issue #4019).

parameters.name: sends
parameters.summary: The sends Thread}}) started, each with the pad it goes to.

parameters.name: leftOut
parameters.summary: Receives the sinks the wait leaves out.

methods.name: ReleaseSendPads
methods.summary: Drops the reference each entry of sends holds on its pad (Thread}})).

methods.name: LogEosWalkFailed
methods.summary: Reports a Thread}}) whose walk over the sources did not finish.

methods.name: InjectEosOnOutputSinks
methods.summary: Pushes EOS onto the muxer's sink pads when the graph could not be resumed to PLAYING after a source error. The output block's own Input is typically the encoder ghost, and an encoder in READY will not forward EOS to mp4mux.

methods.name: InjectEosTowardMuxer
methods.summary: Walks downstream from an output-block input pad to the muxer (element whose src feeds a leaf sink) and EOSes that muxer's sink pads. Falls back to the input pad itself when there is no muxer (a raw filesink output).

parameters.name: inputPad
parameters.summary: The output block's sink pad to start the walk from.

parameters.name: eosSinkNeverPrerolled
parameters.summary: Whether PLAYING is still pending for this graph, i.e. the leaf sinks never accepted a buffer. The fallback pad-EOS is then skipped, and so is any element in front of a sink that would pass the EOS on to it - a capsfilter before an appsink, say; only a muxer built on GstAggregator is EOSed. The skip dates from when the EOS went on the stop thread, where such a sink held it in preroll wait forever (issue #2294). Every EOS sent here goes from a thread of its own (IntPtr)), so none of these can hold the stop.

methods.name: SendEosOffStopThread
methods.summary: Sends EOS to pad from a thread of its own. A serialized event waits for the pad's stream lock (gstpad.c 1.28 gst_pad_send_event_unchecked), and in a graph short of PLAYING that lock can be held for good by a streaming thread blocked behind a prerolled sink - inside a full GstAggregator pad, say (issue #2350). Sent from the stop thread, the EOS would keep the forced NULL that releases it from ever running.

parameters.name: pad
parameters.summary: The pad. The send holds its own reference on it, so the teardown can run underneath.

methods.name: StartEosOffStopThread
methods.summary: IntPtr), returning the thread the send runs on.
methods.returns: The started thread.

methods.name: IsMuxerFeedingSink
methods.summary: An element with both sink and src pads whose src is linked to a leaf sink (filesink, etc.) is the muxer in an encoder → muxer → filesink chain.

methods.name: EosMuxerDownstream
methods.summary: EOSes the sink pads of the first muxer downstream of element. Each element on the way is wrapped only while it is walked, so the muxer is EOSed inside that walk (#2079).

parameters.name: element
parameters.summary: The element to start the walk from.

parameters.name: aggregatorOnly
parameters.summary: EOS only a GstAggregator; walk past every other element.

methods.returns: true when a muxer was found.

methods.name: TrySendEosToSources
methods.summary: Sends EOS to each source child of pipeline, bypassing any whose subtree posted an error. Returns false when the iterator failed or a source could not be wrapped, so some source got no EOS; no pipeline-wide send follows, as it would hold the pipeline's state lock or reach a failed source.

methods.name: SourceTreePostedError
methods.summary: True when source itself, or any child of it, is in the error-handle snapshot. A failed walk of a bin is treated as a match: sending EOS into that bin is the AV we are avoiding.

methods.name: InjectEosDownstreamOf
methods.summary: Pushes EOS on the peer of each linked src pad, so the rest of the branch finalizes without entering the failed element's send_event. Pads come from getters / iterators and are not disposed (one-wrapper-per-pointer cache).

parameters.name: offStopThreads
parameters.summary: Where each EOS sent from a thread of its own (IntPtr)) adds the pad it goes to with that thread; null to send them from this thread.

events.name: OnError

events.name: OnStart

events.name: OnPause
events.summary: Event raised when the pipeline is paused, temporarily suspending media processing. The pipeline can be resumed from the current position without losing state.

events.name: OnReady
events.summary: Event raised when the pipeline has completed initialization and is ready for operation. This indicates that all blocks have been configured and the pipeline is prepared to start.

events.name: OnResume
events.summary: Event raised when the pipeline resumes processing after being paused. Media processing continues from the position where it was paused.

events.name: OnStop
events.summary: Event raised when the pipeline stops media processing, either normally or due to an error. Provides information about the final position and reason for stopping.

events.name: OnLoop
events.summary: Event raised when the pipeline completes processing and automatically restarts due to the Loop property being enabled. This allows for continuous playback of media content.

events.name: OnNetworkSourceDisconnect

events.name: OnBusStreamCollection
events.summary: Event raised when stream collection information becomes available from the pipeline bus. Provides detailed information about all video, audio, and subtitle streams in the media content.

events.name: OnBusStreamsSelected
events.summary: Raised when GStreamer posts GST_MESSAGE_STREAMS_SELECTED with the streams that are actually active. Payload is the selected stream-id list, not the full collection. Internal: MediaPlayerCoreX uses it to keep SELECT_STREAMS sibling-preserving.

classes.name: NVDataDownloadBlock
classes.summary: NVIDIA data download block for transferring video data from GPU to system memory. This block efficiently downloads video frames from NVIDIA GPU memory (CUDA) back to system memory for further processing or output. It's an essential component in GPU-accelerated pipelines where data needs to be transferred from GPU after hardware processing. Supports high-performance memory transfers with minimal CPU overhead, optimized for NVIDIA CUDA architecture. Commonly used after GPU-based video processing, encoding, or effects to bring data back for CPU processing or display. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: VideoStabilizationBlock
classes.summary: Real-time video stabilization (deshake) block. Removes camera shake from a live or file video stream by estimating global inter-frame motion (translation and rotation) with sparse optical flow, smoothing the resulting camera trajectory with a causal moving-average window, and warping each frame back onto the smoothed path. A small centre zoom (crop ratio) hides the borders exposed by compensation. Latency is zero - only past frames are used for smoothing. Backed by the OpenCV vfdeshake GStreamer element, so it requires the OpenCV SDK redistributable (currently Windows, macOS, Mac Catalyst and iOS). Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IVideoProcessingBlock, so the block can also be inserted into a VideoCaptureCoreX / MediaPlayerCoreX video chain with Video_Processing_AddBlock. Implements the IDisposable.

methods.name: ApplySettings
methods.summary: Applies the current Settings to the running element. The vfdeshake element re-reads its properties every frame, so this retunes the stabilization live (enable/disable, smoothing radius, crop ratio, limits) without rebuilding the pipeline. No-op until the block has been built, and after it has been disposed.
methods.remarks: Safe to call from any thread. When the block runs inside an X engine the engine disposes it from a pipeline thread, so the retune is serialized against that disposal.

Simulates the visual distortion seen when looking through hot air, such as heat rising from pavement or fire, creating dynamic wavering and shimmering effects that add realism to hot environments and thermal scenarios. The block is self-contained: it uploads system-memory input to OpenGL and downloads the result back to system memory, so it works between regular video blocks - explicit GLUploadBlock / GLDownloadBlock blocks around it are optional. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

methods.name: Update
methods.summary: Updates the shader programs and uniform variables with the current settings. Recompiles and reloads GLSL shader code and applies new uniform variable values for dynamic shader effects.
methods.remarks: The element is rebuilt rather than reconfigured because glshader does not recompile from its vertex / fragment properties once it holds a shader: with no create-shader handler installed, _maybe_recompile_shader hands the existing shader straight back. Uniforms alone would apply in place; the shader source does not.
methods.returns: true when the new settings are live. false when they are not, and the block keeps running the shader it had: the block is not built yet, the replacement element could not be created, or the swap was refused because the old element could not be taken out of the data flow in time. The last one is what a paused pipeline gives - a sink holding a buffer in preroll keeps a streaming thread inside the chain, and stopping the element under that thread is the deadlock of GitHub issue #838. Push the settings again after resuming.

classes.name: GLVideoMixerBlock
classes.summary: OpenGL-accelerated video mixer block for high-performance multi-stream video compositing and blending. Provides GPU-accelerated video mixing capabilities with multiple input streams, real-time positioning, scaling, rotation, alpha blending, chroma key effects, and advanced compositing operations for live streaming and video production. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: GLXRayBlock
classes.summary: OpenGL-accelerated X-ray visual effect block for creating medical imaging and skeletal visualization effects. Applies GPU-accelerated X-ray transformations that invert colors, enhance edges, and create high-contrast skeletal imagery simulating medical X-ray imaging, with artistic applications for dramatic visual effects and scientific visualizations. classes.name: OGGSpeexOutputBlock
classes.summary: OGG Speex output block for creating compressed voice audio files optimized for speech content. This block combines Speex audio encoding with OGG container packaging, providing an efficient solution for voice recording, VoIP applications, and speech archival. Speex is specifically designed for speech compression, offering superior quality at low bitrates compared to general-purpose audio codecs. The OGG container provides an open, patent-free format with excellent streaming capabilities and metadata support. Key features: - Ultra-efficient speech compression (2-44 kbps) - Voice Activity Detection (VAD) for silence suppression - Variable bitrate (VBR) encoding for optimal quality/size ratio - Wideband (16 kHz) and ultra-wideband (32 kHz) support - Acoustic echo cancellation compatibility - Packet loss concealment for streaming applications Common use cases: - Voice recording and dictation systems - Podcast production with speech-only content - VoIP and telecommunication applications - Audio books and spoken word archives - Voice memo and note-taking applications - Language learning materials While Speex has been largely superseded by Opus for new applications, it remains valuable for legacy system compatibility and specific speech-only scenarios where its optimizations provide benefits. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: OGGVorbisOutputBlock
classes.summary: OGG Vorbis output block for creating high-quality compressed audio files using the open-source Vorbis codec. This block combines Vorbis audio encoding with OGG container packaging, providing an excellent solution for music distribution, streaming audio, and multimedia content creation. Vorbis offers superior audio quality compared to MP3 at similar bitrates, making it ideal for applications where audio fidelity is paramount. The OGG container provides a patent-free, open standard format with robust streaming capabilities and comprehensive metadata support. Key features: - High-quality lossy audio compression (45-500 kbps) - Superior sound quality at low to medium bitrates - Variable bitrate (VBR) encoding for optimal quality/size ratio - Support for sample rates up to 192 kHz - Multi-channel audio support (mono to 7.1 surround) - Comprehensive metadata tagging (Vorbis comments) - Streaming-optimized container format Common use cases: - Music distribution and archival - Game audio assets and soundtracks - Podcast and audiobook production - Web audio streaming applications - Open-source multimedia projects - Cross-platform audio solutions Vorbis remains an excellent choice for applications requiring patent-free, high-quality audio compression with broad platform support and superior performance at medium bitrates. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

methods.summary: Ends a live push counted in _livePushes and wakes a DestroyOutputPipeline waiting for it.

methods.name: OnEncodedVideoSample
methods.summary: Handles new encoded video samples from the appsink. Stores frame data in the circular buffer and optionally forwards to the output pipeline.

methods.name: OnEncodedAudioSample
methods.summary: Handles new encoded audio samples from the appsink.

methods.name: NoteStreamFormat
methods.summary: Stores the stream format from caps, or adopts a new one. The fast path does not take _outputLock. A real change does, and it takes that lock before _stateLock.

methods.name: ApplyFormatChange
methods.summary: Adopts format for one stream. The first sample only stores it. A later change drops that stream's buffered frames and, when a file is open, finalizes it so the file holds one format. The other stream's buffer stays. Must not be called under either lock.

methods.name: PushEncodedBufferToAppSrc
methods.summary: Pushes encoded frame data to a GStreamer appsrc element. A live push was counted in _livePushes by the caller and is released here, before anything is reported: a log sink that stops the block waits in DestroyOutputPipeline for that count.

methods.name: TriggerRecording
methods.summary: Triggers recording: flushes the pre-event buffer to a file and continues recording live frames. If already recording, extends the current recording (resets the post-event timer). The call is refused until the first encoded video sample has arrived and, when audio is enabled, until the first encoded audio sample has arrived.

parameters.name: filename
parameters.summary: The output filename for the recording.

methods.name: RaiseUnraisedEvents
methods.summary: Raises the events queued in _unraisedEvents, in order, outside both locks: a handler that waits on a thread calling Stop would deadlock under them. Returns at once when another thread is raising them, including this thread from inside a handler: that thread raises these too, after the events before them.

methods.name: QueueStopEvents
methods.summary: Queues a stop's events behind the ones not raised yet: OnStateChanged, then OnRecordingStopped when a file was finalized (filename is not null). Must be called under _outputLock, after DestroyOutputPipeline closed the file; takes _stateLock.

methods.name: RaiseQueuedEvents
methods.summary: Raises the queued events and rethrows what their handlers threw. Nothing when another thread is raising them: that thread raises these too.

methods.name: RaiseQueuedEventsLogged
methods.summary: RaiseQueuedEvents for the callers that cannot let a handler's exception escape; reports it through Context.Error instead.

methods.name: RaiseCollecting
methods.summary: Raises one event; what its handler throws is added to errors.

methods.name: ThrowHandlerErrors
methods.summary: Rethrows what the event handlers threw: one exception as it was, several as an AggregateException.

methods.name: BeginRecordingLocked
methods.summary: Phase 1 of a trigger: validates the state, drains the buffer and switches to Recording. Must be called under _outputLock. Returns false when nothing was started (extended or refused).

methods.name: SetUpRecordingLocked
methods.summary: Phases 2 and 3 of a trigger: builds and fills the output pipeline and starts the post-event timer. Must be called under _outputLock. Queues its events in _unraisedEvents.

methods.name: AbandonSetUpLocked
methods.summary: Abandons a trigger whose setup failed: destroys the output and goes back to Buffering, so the block does not stay in Recording queueing live frames with no timer to stop it. Must be called under _outputLock. Queues the Buffering event in _unraisedEvents.

methods.name: DisposePendingLiveFramesLocked
methods.summary: Drops the live frames queued for an output that is not ready. Must be called under _stateLock.

methods.name: ExtendRecording
methods.summary: Extends the current recording by resetting the post-event timer. Call this when the trigger condition is still active (e.g., motion continues).

methods.name: StopRecording
methods.summary: Manually stops the current recording and returns to buffering mode.

methods.name: StopBuffering
methods.summary: Stops everything including buffering. Clears the buffer. The block stays Stopped, across pipeline restarts, until StartBuffering. A repeated call raises no event.

methods.name: StartBuffering
methods.summary: Starts or resumes buffering after being stopped. Frames are buffered only while the pipeline runs. Called before the pipeline starts, it raises OnStateChanged(Buffering) at once and the start does not raise it again. Does nothing when the block is already buffering or is disposed.

methods.name: TryStop
methods.summary: The one stop path: when precondition holds under _stateLock and the block is not already in newState (a repeated call raises nothing), finalizes a recording in progress, optionally clears the buffer and moves to newState. Waits for a trigger still setting up or a teardown already running on another thread, so the file is complete when this returns. Raises nothing: queues its events behind the ones not raised yet, for RaiseQueuedEvents. Returns false when the block is disposed, the precondition did not hold or the block was already in newState.

methods.name: IsValidPostEventDuration
methods.summary: Whether postEvent is a duration System.Threading.Timer takes; reports it through Context.Error when not. Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan records until StopRecording.

methods.name: IsCurrentSetUp
methods.summary: Whether the trigger id is still the one setting up. Must be called under _outputLock; takes _stateLock.

methods.name: IsRecordingLocked
methods.summary: Whether a recording is set up or in its post-event part. Must be called under _stateLock.

methods.name: OnPostEventTimerElapsed
methods.summary: Post-event timer callback - stops recording when the timer elapses.

methods.name: StopRecordingInternalLocked
methods.summary: Internal method to stop recording state. Must be called under _outputLock and _stateLock. Sets state to Buffering and disposes the timer, but does NOT call DestroyOutputPipeline or raise OnStateChanged — the caller MUST destroy after releasing _stateLock but before releasing _outputLock, and raise the events after releasing both. Returns the filename of the stopped recording for event notification, or null when the stop came between a trigger's two phases, before its file was created.

methods.summary: Creates the dynamic output pipeline for recording.

methods.name: FlushFramesToOutput
methods.summary: Flushes pre-event video and audio frames to the output pipeline separately, preserving decode order within each stream.

methods.name: DestroyOutputPipeline
methods.summary: Destroys the dynamic output pipeline.

methods.name: RaiseStateChanged
methods.summary: Fires the state changed event. Never called under _stateLock: a handler that waits on a thread reading State would deadlock.

classes.summary: WMV output block for creating Windows Media Video files with integrated WMV video and WMA audio encoding. This block provides comprehensive Windows Media Format support, combining Microsoft's proprietary video and audio codecs in an ASF container. WMV offers excellent compression efficiency and is widely supported on Windows platforms, making it ideal for Windows-centric workflows, corporate environments, and legacy system compatibility. Key features: - WMV video compression (VC-1 codec) with multiple profiles - WMA audio compression with various quality levels - ASF container with rich metadata support - DRM (Digital Rights Management) capability - Variable bitrate (VBR) and constant bitrate (CBR) encoding - Multiple video profiles (Simple, Main, Advanced) - Support for HD content up to 1080p Common use cases: - Windows Media Player content distribution - Corporate video presentations and training - Silverlight streaming applications - Xbox and Windows device playback - Legacy Windows media workflows - Protected content distribution with DRM While newer formats like H.264/MP4 have largely superseded WMV, it remains valuable for Windows-specific applications and legacy system compatibility where Windows Media support is guaranteed. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: RTSPServerBlock
classes.summary: RTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol) server sink block that streams audio/video content over a network. This block creates an RTSP server endpoint that clients can connect to for receiving live or recorded media streams. It supports H.264/H.265 video and various audio codecs, providing standard-compliant RTSP streaming with RTP/RTCP transport protocols. The server handles multiple client connections simultaneously, supports RTSP authentication, and provides low-latency streaming suitable for security cameras, live broadcasting, and media distribution. Features include configurable port binding, custom mount points, multicast support, bandwidth management, and client session tracking. Compatible with standard RTSP clients including VLC, FFmpeg, GStreamer, and IP camera viewers. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: ASFSinkBlock
classes.summary: ASF (Advanced Systems Format) sink block for writing media streams to ASF/WMV/WMA container files.
classes.remarks: The ASF sink block supports writing audio and video streams to the Advanced Systems Format container, commonly used for Windows Media files (.wmv for video, .wma for audio, .asf for generic content). This format is optimized for streaming and supports advanced features like DRM, multiple bitrates, and metadata embedding. Key Features:Support for multiple audio and video streamsWindows Media Video (WMV) and Windows Media Audio (WMA) codec supportMetadata and tagging supportSuitable for both local file storage and streaming scenariosCompatible with Windows Media Player and other ASF-compliant playersTypical Use Cases:Creating Windows Media files for playback on Windows systemsRecording video content for streaming over Windows Media ServicesArchiving media in a format with good compression and quality balanceCreating content for legacy Windows-based media systemsLimitations:Limited codec support (primarily WMV/WMA codecs)Less universal playback support compared to MP4 or MKVProprietary format with potential licensing considerations

classes.name: BufferSinkBlock
classes.summary: Implements a sink block that captures media data into memory buffers for processing or analysis. Provides frame-by-frame access to video, audio, or raw data through event callbacks.
classes.remarks: The BufferSinkBlock is designed for scenarios where you need direct access to media frames in memory rather than writing to a file. It supports: - Video frame capture with format conversion - Audio frame capture with resampling - Raw data capture for custom media types - Frame dropping for performance optimization - Synchronization control for playback vs transcoding Frame data is delivered through event callbacks, allowing real-time processing, analysis, or custom rendering. The block can be configured to drop frames when the processing cannot keep up with the media rate. Common use cases include: - Video frame analysis and processing - Audio visualization - Custom rendering implementations - Media stream monitoring - Frame extraction for thumbnails

classes.name: DASHSinkBlock
classes.summary: DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) sink block for creating adaptive streaming content.
classes.remarks: The DASH sink block generates MPEG-DASH content, an international standard for adaptive bitrate streaming. DASH works by breaking the overall stream into a sequence of small HTTP-based file segments, each representing a short interval of playback time. This enables adaptive streaming, VOD, and live broadcasts. Key Features:Adaptive bitrate streaming supportAutomatic generation of MPD (Media Presentation Description) manifest filesConfigurable segment duration and buffering parametersSupport for both live and on-demand contentCompatible with all major browsers and streaming platformsMulti-period support for different quality levelsTypical Use Cases:Live streaming to browsers and mobile devicesCreating VOD content for web-based video playersBuilding adaptive streaming solutionsStreaming to smart TVs and set-top boxesCDN-friendly content distributionTechnical Specifications:Segment format: ISO BMFF (fragmented MP4) filesVideo codecs: H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, VP9, AV1Audio codecs: AAC, MP3, OpusManifest format: MPD (Media Presentation Description) XMLDefault segment duration: 5 seconds (configurable)Output Structure: The sink creates a directory structure with an MPD manifest file and segment files. For live streaming, old segments are automatically removed based on time shift buffer settings.

Key features: - MISB (Motion Imagery Standards Board) compliant metadata handling - STANAG 4609 compatible encoding - Synchronous metadata storage with video streams - Support for various KLV data types and structures KLV metadata typically includes: - GPS coordinates and altitude - Camera orientation (pan, tilt, roll) - Platform information (aircraft, drone, vehicle) - Timestamp and synchronization data - Target tracking information - Environmental data (weather, visibility) Common use cases: - UAV/Drone video metadata recording - Surveillance system metadata storage - Military and defense applications - Geospatial video indexing - Compliance with government standards The sink writes raw KLV data that can be multiplexed with video or stored separately for later synchronization.

classes.name: MKVSinkBlock
classes.summary: MKV (Matroska) sink block for creating highly flexible multimedia container files.
classes.remarks: The MKV sink block creates Matroska files, one of the most flexible and feature-rich multimedia container formats available. Matroska is an open-source format that can hold an unlimited number of video, audio, subtitle, and metadata tracks in a single file. It's particularly popular for high-quality video archiving and distribution. Key Features:Support for virtually any video and audio codecMultiple video, audio, and subtitle tracks in one fileChapter markers and navigation menusMetadata and tag support (title, artist, etc.)Error recovery features for damaged filesVariable framerate supportAttachments (fonts, images, etc.)Streaming capability over HTTPTypical Use Cases:High-quality video archiving and preservationMulti-language video distribution (multiple audio/subtitle tracks)Anime and foreign film distribution with subtitlesProfessional video production workflowsCreating files with multiple camera anglesLong-duration recordings that may need error recoveryTechnical Specifications:Based on EBML (Extensible Binary Meta Language)No inherent resolution or bitrate limitationsSupports all common codecs: H.264, H.265, VP9, AV1, AAC, FLAC, etc.Subtitle formats: SRT, SSA/ASS, VobSub, and morePrecise timestamp handling with nanosecond accuracyAdvantages over other containers: MKV offers more features than MP4 but may have less universal playback support. It's ideal when flexibility and features are more important than compatibility. Modern players and devices increasingly support MKV natively.

classes.summary: Implements a sink block for writing media to QuickTime MOV container files. Supports multiple video and audio tracks with Apple-compatible codecs.
classes.remarks: The MOVSinkBlock creates QuickTime movie files (.mov), Apple's multimedia container format. classes.name: MP4SinkBlock
classes.summary: MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 14) sink block for writing media streams to MP4 container files.
classes.remarks: The MP4 sink block provides comprehensive support for creating MP4 files, the industry-standard container format for digital multimedia. MP4 files can contain video, audio, subtitles, and metadata tracks, making it ideal for a wide range of applications from video recording to streaming content preparation. Key Features:Support for multiple video and audio tracksCompatible with H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, AAC, MP3, and other codecsFast-start support for progressive download/streamingFragmented MP4 support for live streaming scenariosMetadata and chapter supportMux-only mode for remuxing pre-encoded streamsSplit recording capability for file size managementTypical Use Cases:Recording camera feeds to standard video filesCreating content for web streaming platformsProducing files for mobile device playbackArchiving video content in a universally compatible formatPreparing content for video editing workflowsTechnical Specifications:Compliant with ISO/IEC 14496-14 standardMaximum file size: Limited by filesystem (typically 4GB on FAT32)Supports both constant and variable bitrate encodingCompatible with all major media players and editing software

classes.name: NDISinkBlock
classes.summary: NDI (Network Device Interface) sink block for broadcasting video over IP networks.
classes.remarks: The NDI sink block enables high-quality, low-latency video transmission over standard Ethernet networks using NewTek's NDI protocol. NDI has become the de facto standard for IP video production, allowing multiple video systems to identify and communicate with one another over IP, and to encode, transmit, and receive high-quality video with minimal latency. Key Features:Ultra-low latency transmission (typically 1 frame)Automatic network discovery of NDI sourcesSupport for full resolution video with alpha channelMulti-channel audio supportBi-directional metadata communicationMulticast and unicast transmission modesHardware acceleration support on compatible systemsTypical Use Cases:Live production workflows in broadcast environmentsMulti-camera productions without physical SDI/HDMI cablesRemote production and contribution feedsVirtual sets and augmented reality applicationsVideo conferencing and collaboration systemsDigital signage and display wallsTechnical Requirements:NDI Runtime (v5 or v6) must be installed on the systemGigabit Ethernet network recommended (100 Mbps minimum)Video formats: Various resolutions up to 4K and beyondAudio: Up to 16 channels of float32 audioColor formats: UYVY, BGRA, RGBA with optional alphaPlatform Notes: The implementation differs between platforms. On Windows, it may use direct NDI SDK integration, while on other platforms it uses GStreamer's NDI plugin. The NDI_RUNTIME_DIR_V5 or NDI_RUNTIME_DIR_V6 environment variable must be set.

classes.remarks: The RTMP sink block enables live streaming of audio and video content to RTMP-compatible streaming servers and platforms. methods.name: RequestStop
methods.summary: Signals the block that the pipeline is stopping. Disables the native sink's auto-reconnect so a streaming thread parked in the reconnect loop against an unreachable peer exits within one poll interval instead of spinning forever - otherwise EOS delivery (which needs that streaming thread) blocks StopAsync indefinitely. The prompt exit needs a native SRT plugin that honors a mid-flight switch-off; the macOS redist ships a patched libgstsrt.dylib (#879), the Windows redist a patched gstsrt.dll (#1190), and the Android and iOS redists a patched srt plugin built into libgstreamer_android.so (#1350) and GStreamerX.framework (#1349). Stock GStreamer builds capture the setting once per write call, so the loop ends only from the next call.

classes.name: WAVSinkBlock
classes.summary: WAV sink block for writing uncompressed audio data to WAV (Waveform Audio File Format) files.
classes.remarks: The WAV sink block creates standard WAV files containing uncompressed PCM audio data. WAV is the de facto standard for high-quality audio storage on Windows systems and is widely supported across all platforms. It provides perfect audio fidelity at the cost of larger file sizes compared to compressed formats. Key Features:Uncompressed PCM audio for perfect qualitySupport for various bit depths (8, 16, 24, 32-bit)Multiple sample rates (8kHz to 192kHz and beyond)Mono, stereo, and multi-channel supportStandard RIFF/WAV file structureMetadata support through INFO chunksNo quality loss or compression artifactsTypical Use Cases:Professional audio recording and productionAudio archiving with maximum qualityIntermediate format for audio processing workflowsVoice recording for transcription or analysisScientific audio data captureAudio mastering and post-productionTechnical Specifications:Container: RIFF (Resource Interchange File Format)Audio format: Linear PCM (uncompressed)Bit depths: 8, 16, 24, or 32-bit integer; 32-bit floatChannels: 1 (mono), 2 (stereo), or more for surroundMaximum file size: 4GB (due to 32-bit RIFF header)Byte order: Little-endianLimitations: Standard WAV files are limited to 4GB due to the 32-bit file size field in the RIFF header. For larger files, consider using RF64/WAV64 format or splitting into multiple files. The lack of compression means significantly larger file sizes compared to formats like MP3 or AAC.

classes.name: WebMSinkBlock
classes.summary: WebM sink block for creating WebM container files with VP8/VP9 video and Vorbis/Opus audio.
classes.remarks: The WebM sink block creates WebM files, an open-source multimedia container format designed specifically for the web. WebM is based on a subset of the Matroska (MKV) container and is optimized for streaming over the internet. It's particularly popular for HTML5 video delivery due to its royalty-free codecs and broad browser support. Key Features:Support for VP8 and VP9 video codecsSupport for Vorbis and Opus audio codecsOptimized for web streaming and HTML5 videoRoyalty-free format with no licensing feesMetadata and chapter supportEfficient compression with good qualityNative browser support in Chrome, Firefox, Opera, and EdgeTypical Use Cases:Creating video content for web platformsHTML5 video embedding without plugin requirementsOpen-source video distributionStreaming video content with adaptive bitrateCreating royalty-free video archivesTechnical Specifications:Container: Based on Matroska (MKV) formatVideo codecs: VP8 (older), VP9 (recommended for better compression)Audio codecs: Vorbis (older), Opus (recommended for better quality)Maximum resolution: No inherent limit (4K and beyond supported)Streaming: Supports progressive download and adaptive streamingBrowser Compatibility: WebM is natively supported in most modern browsers without plugins. For maximum compatibility, consider providing fallback formats like MP4.

It handles the specific requirements of YouTube Live, including proper RTMP formatting, recommended encoding settings, and stream key management. This sink simplifies the process of broadcasting to YouTube without manually configuring generic RTMP parameters. Key Features:Direct integration with YouTube Live streamingAutomatic RTMP URL construction from stream keyPre-configured for YouTube's recommended settingsSupport for scheduled live events and instant streamingCompatible with YouTube's Content ID systemAutomatic reconnection on network interruptionsTypical Use Cases:Live streaming gaming sessionsBroadcasting webinars and online events24/7 continuous streaming channelsLive podcasts and talk showsEducational content and tutorialsLive product demonstrationsTechnical Requirements:Video codec: H.264 (required by YouTube)Audio codec: AAC or MP3Recommended bitrates: 2.5-4 Mbps for 720p, 4.5-9 Mbps for 1080pMaximum resolution: 4K (3840x2160) at 60 fpsKeyframe interval: 2 seconds (required)Valid YouTube stream key from YouTube StudioSetup Requirements: To use this sink, you need to enable live streaming in your YouTube account and obtain a stream key from YouTube Studio. classes.remarks: The H264ParseBlock processes H.264 encoded video streams, parsing NAL (Network Abstraction Layer) units, extracting SPS/PPS parameters, and ensuring proper access unit boundaries. H.264 is the most widely adopted video codec for streaming, broadcasting, and video storage. Key features: - NAL unit parsing and validation (start codes and length-prefixed) - SPS (Sequence Parameter Set) and PPS (Picture Parameter Set) extraction - Access unit boundary detection based on H.264 specification - SEI (Supplemental Enhancement Information) message parsing - Slice header analysis for frame type detection - Support for both Annex B (start codes) and AVCC (length-prefixed) formats Common use cases: - Streaming: Preparing H.264 for HLS, DASH, or RTP transmission - Muxing: Packaging H.264 into MP4, MKV, or TS containers - Analysis: Extracting codec parameters and stream properties - Transcoding: Providing properly parsed NAL units to decoders - Video editing: Frame-accurate cutting and splicing The parser handles various H.264 profiles (Baseline, Main, High) and levels, automatically adapting to the stream's characteristics and ensuring compliance with the H.264 specification (ITU-T H.264 / ISO/IEC 14496-10).

classes.summary: Parses H.265/HEVC (High Efficiency Video Coding) bitstreams for NAL unit processing and frame boundary detection.
classes.remarks: The H265ParseBlock processes H.265/HEVC encoded video streams, parsing NAL (Network Abstraction Layer) units, extracting VPS/SPS/PPS parameters, and ensuring proper access unit boundaries. H.265 offers approximately 50% better compression than H.264 while maintaining similar video quality. Key features: - NAL unit parsing with support for multi-layer extensions - VPS (Video Parameter Set), SPS, and PPS extraction - Access unit boundary detection per HEVC specification - Temporal layer identification and scalability support - SEI message parsing including HDR metadata (HDR10, HLG) - Support for both Annex B and HVCC (length-prefixed) formats - Slice segment header analysis for frame type detection Common use cases: - Streaming: Preparing HEVC for HLS, DASH, or RTP transmission - Muxing: Packaging HEVC into MP4, MKV, or TS containers - HDR processing: Extracting and preserving HDR metadata - Transcoding: Providing properly parsed NAL units to HEVC decoders - 4K/8K video: Handling high-resolution video streams efficiently The parser handles various HEVC profiles including Main, Main 10, Main Still Picture, and Range Extensions. It automatically detects stream characteristics including bit depth, chroma format, and HDR signaling.

classes.name: JPEG2000ParseBlock

classes.remarks: The JPEG2000ParseBlock processes JPEG 2000 encoded image and video streams, identifying codestream markers, extracting header information, and ensuring proper frame segmentation. classes.summary: Parses MPEG-1 and MPEG-2 video elementary streams for picture boundary detection and header analysis.
classes.remarks: The MPEG12VideoParseBlock processes MPEG-1 and MPEG-2 video elementary streams, identifying picture start codes, extracting sequence and picture headers, and ensuring proper GOP (Group of Pictures) alignment. Key features: - Start code detection and validation (picture, sequence, GOP) - Sequence header parsing (resolution, frame rate, aspect ratio) - Picture header analysis (I, P, B frame types) - GOP structure identification and temporal reference - Extension header parsing for MPEG-2 features - Progressive and interlaced content handling - Closed caption data extraction when present Common use cases: - DVD playback: Processing MPEG-2 video from DVD sources - Broadcasting: Handling MPEG-2 streams from DVB/ATSC systems - Legacy conversion: Transcoding MPEG-1/2 to modern formats - Video analysis: Extracting GOP structure and frame types - Muxing: Preparing elementary streams for program streams or transport streams The parser supports various MPEG-2 profiles and levels including Main Profile @ Main Level (MP@ML) for SD content and Main Profile @ High Level (MP@HL) for HD content. It handles both MPEG-1 constrained parameters and full MPEG-2 feature sets.

classes.name: MPEG4ParseBlock
classes.summary: Parses MPEG-4 Part 2 (MPEG-4 Visual) bitstreams for VOP boundary detection and codec parameter extraction.
classes.remarks: The MPEG4ParseBlock processes MPEG-4 Part 2 encoded video streams, parsing Visual Object Sequences (VOS), Visual Object Layer (VOL) headers, and Video Object Planes (VOPs) to ensure proper frame boundaries. classes.name: PNGParseBlock
classes.summary: Parses PNG (Portable Network Graphics) image streams for chunk validation and metadata extraction.
classes.remarks: The PNGParseBlock processes PNG image streams, parsing the chunk-based structure to validate image integrity and extract metadata. PNG is a lossless image format widely used for web graphics, screenshots, and images requiring transparency support. Key features: - PNG signature validation (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A) - Critical chunk parsing: IHDR, PLTE, IDAT, IEND - Ancillary chunk support: tEXt, iTXt, gAMA, cHRM, sRGB, etc. - CRC-32 validation for each chunk - Interlaced PNG support (Adam7 interlacing) - Color type detection (grayscale, RGB, palette, alpha) - Bit depth validation (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 bits per channel) - APNG (Animated PNG) frame detection Common use cases: - Image processing: Validating PNG files before decoding - Streaming: Extracting PNG images from video or data streams - Metadata extraction: Reading text chunks and color space information - Format conversion: Preparing PNG data for transcoding - Web applications: Processing uploaded PNG images - Animation: Handling APNG sequences The parser ensures PNG specification compliance (ISO/IEC 15948:2003) and handles various PNG variants including standard PNG, APNG (animated), and PNG with extensive metadata. It validates chunk ordering and detects malformed files.

classes.name: VC1ParseBlock
classes.summary: Parses VC-1/WMV3 (Windows Media Video) bitstreams for frame boundary detection and codec parameter extraction.
classes.remarks: The VC1ParseBlock processes VC-1 encoded video streams, parsing Sequence Layer Headers, Entry Point Headers, and Picture Headers to ensure proper frame boundaries. VC-1 is Microsoft's video codec standard (SMPTE 421M) used in WMV9, HD DVD, and Blu-ray. Key features: - Sequence Layer Header parsing for codec profile and level detection - Entry Point Header processing for display parameters - Picture Header analysis for frame type determination (I, P, B, BI) - Support for Simple, Main, and Advanced Profiles - Handles both ASF encapsulated and raw VC-1 bitstreams - Frame boundary detection based on VC-1 specification - Interlaced and progressive content support Common use cases: - Streaming: Processing WMV content for adaptive streaming - Muxing: Packaging VC-1 into ASF, MP4, or MKV containers - Transcoding: Providing properly parsed frames to VC-1 decoders - Broadcast: Handling VC-1 streams in broadcast applications - Media analysis: Extracting codec parameters and stream properties The parser handles all VC-1 profiles including Simple Profile (WMV9 Simple), Main Profile (WMV9 Main), and Advanced Profile (WVC1), automatically adapting to the stream characteristics and ensuring compliance with SMPTE 421M.

classes.name: VP9ParseBlock
classes.summary: Parses VP9 video bitstreams for superframe boundary detection and codec parameter extraction.
classes.remarks: The VP9ParseBlock processes VP9 encoded video streams, parsing frame headers and superframe structures to ensure proper frame boundaries. VP9 is Google's open-source video codec offering efficient compression for web video, competing with H.265/HEVC while remaining royalty-free. Key features: - Superframe parsing and frame boundary detection - Frame header parsing for resolution and reference frame info (forwarded as downstream caps) - Show existing frame and invisible frame handling Properties of the bitstream that the underlying vp9parse element inspects (profile, scalability layers, segmentation, HDR / colour metadata) are not surfaced on this wrapper as a managed API — they affect negotiated caps and downstream behaviour, not the block's public surface. Common use cases: - Streaming: Preparing VP9 for WebM/DASH adaptive streaming - Muxing: Packaging VP9 into WebM, MP4, or MKV containers - Web video: Processing VP9 content for HTML5 video playback - Transcoding: Providing properly parsed frames to VP9 decoders - YouTube: Handling VP9 streams from YouTube and similar platforms - WebRTC: Processing VP9 in real-time communication applications The parser supports all VP9 profiles: - Profile 0: 8-bit 4:2:0 (most common) - Profile 1: 8-bit 4:2:2, 4:4:4 - Profile 2: 10/12-bit 4:2:0 - Profile 3: 10/12-bit 4:2:2, 4:4:4 It handles both traditional frame-based streams and superframe-packed formats commonly used in WebM containers.

classes.summary: Reads and writes the sources of a video mixer, which are typed by the IVideoMixerSource interface and so carry no CLR type of their own in JSON. The concrete settings class is named by a $type property holding its simple type name.
classes.remarks: The name is resolved against a whitelist built by reflection - the loaded VisioForge assemblies' concrete implementations of - so a document can never name an arbitrary type to instantiate.Half of the source settings classes are compiled per platform, so a document written on Windows can name a source this build does not contain. That is reported as a , which the materializer already turns into an MBS043 naming the block, rather than a null source that would surface much later as a missing mixer pad. matches on the exact type by default, so the nested serialize/deserialize calls below - made against the concrete class - do not re-enter this converter.

methods.remarks: Synchronous, and a document that names an audio device enumerates the machine's devices to match it - a cold enumeration starts a GStreamer device monitor and can take seconds. Call this off the UI thread, or enumerate once beforehand (any DeviceEnumerator.Shared.Audio*Async call warms the cache for the process).

methods.name: AttachDevices
methods.summary: Replaces the device identities a document carries with the live devices this machine has. A document stores what identifies a device - its name, path, API and the platform's own stable id - and never the enumerator's handle, so an audio device read back from JSON arrives detached: matching it here is what makes the numeric CoreAudio id or the WASAPI path current again, rather than whatever it was when the document was written. This is the one step in materialization that talks to the platform's device stack, and the enumeration behind it can take seconds on a cold process. It runs only for a document that actually names a device, and the enumerator caches its result for the process - but see the remarks on before calling it from a UI thread.

Top level only: a path nested inside another settings object - the image a FallbackSwitchSettings falls back to is the one in the tree - is left as written and resolves against the process working directory. Nothing in the editor can produce one: the descriptor exposes top-level properties only, so it takes a hand-edited document.

parameters.name: baseDirectory

classes.summary: Reads and writes a settings hierarchy whose declared type is an interface or an abstract class - so it carries no CLR type of its own in JSON. The concrete settings class is named by a $type property holding its simple type name; without this a document writes the value as an empty object and then refuses to read it back.

An implementation that System.Text.Json cannot construct is left out of that map, which turns "wrote a value nothing can read back" into a diagnostic at write time.Half of the encoder settings classes are compiled per platform, so a document written on Windows can name a class this build does not contain. That is reported as a , which the materializer already turns into an MBS043 naming the block, rather than a null that would surface much later. matches on the exact type by default, so the nested serialize/deserialize calls below - made against the concrete class - do not re-enter this converter.

classes.remarks: One map per hierarchy, shared by every converter that resolves a $type name - the mixer sources and the settings declared as an interface or an abstract base - so the rule is stated once and a class left out is refused at write time rather than saved as an object nothing reads back.The name is resolved against a whitelist built by reflection from the loaded VisioForge assemblies, so a document can never name an arbitrary type to instantiate.

methods.summary: Reports whether JsonSerializer can build this type from a document, by the rules it actually applies: the [JsonConstructor] one, which it honours on a non-public constructor too, else a public parameterless one, else a single public constructor - and every parameter of whichever it picks has to name a public property to take its value from.
methods.remarks: "Has some public constructor" is not the same test and lets classes through that cannot be read back. UniversalSourceSettingsV2 has no public constructor at all, because an async factory probes the media first, and no [JsonConstructor] to stand in for one. A type with two public constructors and neither a parameterless one nor a [JsonConstructor] is a NotSupportedException on read. Excluding them means the write is refused with a diagnostic rather than producing a document that loads into a different composition. The non-public [JsonConstructor] has to count, or this refuses to write what the rest of the stack round-trips: AlliedVisionSourceSettings restores from a document through exactly such a constructor, which is how MediaBlockCatalog materializes it, yet a mixer holding it was refused an entry. The attribute matters on a public constructor too - GenICamSourceSettings has two of those and needs it to say which one binds.

classes.name: ClockSyncBlock
classes.summary: Paces the buffers that pass through it to the pipeline clock at a chosen multiple of real time, without dropping or duplicating any of them. A file-to-file pipeline normally runs as fast as the machine allows; with this block it runs at Rate times real time. The rate paces the processing only: the timestamps and duration of the output are unchanged, so a file written at rate 2 still plays at normal speed. It is not a playback-speed control. The rate is applied when the pipeline starts and stays fixed while it runs. To pace a stream with both audio and video, put one block with the same rate on each branch and leave SyncToFirst off, so both branches are paced against the same running time. The no-drop promise holds for a source that waits for the pipeline, such as a file, and for sinks that do not sync to the clock, such as a file sink or a NullRendererBlock with IsSync off. A live source (camera, network stream) keeps producing in real time, so a rate below 1 backs it up and the frames are dropped upstream of this block. A renderer downstream still plays at real time, because the block forwards the original timestamps: above rate 1 it holds the frames back, below rate 1 it drops them as late. The rate scales one continuous stream. A source that chains segments (a loop, a playlist, a non-flushing seek) is not paced correctly after its first segment: at rate 2 it waits about half of what has played before going on. The pipeline also behaves as a live one: it does not preroll, so a paused pipeline shows no frame, and at rate 1 the element answers the latency query as live, so a mixer downstream aggregates in live mode. The element offers the system clock to the pipeline. Unless an element further upstream provides its own clock, the system clock becomes the pipeline clock, and an audio renderer in the same pipeline is slaved to it. Requires GStreamer 1.28 or newer (see IsAvailable). Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.summary: A specialized media block that detects and decodes DataMatrix 2D barcodes from video frames in real-time. This block analyzes incoming video frames for DataMatrix codes using the LibDMTX library with optimized frame processing, configurable frame skipping, and asynchronous decoding to minimize performance impact on the video pipeline. Key features: - Real-time DataMatrix detection and decoding from video streams - Asynchronous processing with automatic frame dropping if busy - Configurable frame skip to reduce CPU usage (analyze every Nth frame) - Support for multiple DataMatrix codes in a single frame - Event-based notification when DataMatrix codes are detected - Support for various video formats (RGB, BGR, RGBA, BGRA) - Configurable decode timeout and symbol size hints Common use cases: - Industrial tracking with DataMatrix codes on products - Document processing with embedded DataMatrix codes - Inventory management systems - Quality control and verification systems - Medical device and pharmaceutical tracking Technical details: - Uses LibDMTX for DataMatrix detection and decoding - Processes frames asynchronously to avoid blocking the pipeline - Automatically converts video formats to RGB for LibDMTX - Thread-safe with proper synchronization - Supports both passthrough and sink modes Implements the MediaBlock. classes.name: DataSampleGrabberBlock
classes.summary: A specialized media block that intercepts and provides access to raw media data frames passing through the pipeline. This block acts as a transparent passthrough while capturing frame data for analysis, processing, or monitoring. Unlike video/audio-specific grabbers, this block can handle any media type including metadata streams. Key features: - Zero-copy frame access with minimal performance impact - Support for any media type (video, audio, metadata, subtitles) - Passthrough design maintains pipeline flow - Event-based notification for each frame - Access to raw buffer data and timing information - Configurable media type filtering Common use cases: - Capturing metadata streams from specialized sources - Monitoring data flow for debugging purposes - Extracting timing information from media streams - Analyzing proprietary data formats - Building custom analytics on media streams - Implementing data stream validators Technical details: - Uses GStreamer pad probes for non-invasive data access - Provides frame data through event callbacks - Maintains original buffer timestamps and metadata - Can be configured for specific media types or auto-detect - Thread-safe frame delivery via events Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: DecodeBinBlock
classes.summary: An intelligent decoding block that automatically detects and decodes various media formats into raw streams. DecodeBin analyzes incoming media data, identifies the format and codecs, and constructs an appropriate decoding pipeline to produce raw video, audio, and subtitle outputs. Key features: - Automatic format detection and codec selection - Support for virtually any media format GStreamer can decode - Dynamic pad creation for discovered streams - Separate outputs for video, audio, and subtitle streams - Built-in format conversion for consistent output - Configurable stream selection (video/audio/subtitle) Common use cases: - Decoding media files with unknown or variable formats - Processing network streams with dynamic content - Building flexible media players that handle any format - Extracting raw streams from container formats - Media analysis and transcoding pipelines - Multi-stream processing applications Technical details: - Uses GStreamer's decodebin3 element for intelligent decoding (the legacy decodebin via UseLegacyDecodeBin) - Automatically constructs decoder chains based on stream caps - Includes queue elements for each stream to handle threading - Video output includes format conversion to standard formats - Audio output can optionally include format conversion - Handles dynamic stream addition during playback Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: DecryptorBlock
classes.summary: A specialized media block that decrypts AES-encrypted media streams in real-time. This block processes encrypted media data and outputs the decrypted content, enabling secure media distribution and playback of protected content. Key features: - AES decryption with configurable key sizes (128, 192, 256 bits) - Support for various AES modes (ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR, GCM) - Real-time stream decryption with minimal latency - Transparent passthrough design - Compatible with any media type (video, audio, data) - Configurable initialization vectors and padding Common use cases: - Playback of DRM-protected content - Secure media streaming applications - Decrypting downloaded encrypted media files - Building secure media distribution systems - Implementing custom content protection schemes - Compliance with content security requirements Technical details: - Uses hardware-accelerated AES when available - Maintains stream timing and metadata - Zero-copy operation where possible - Thread-safe decryption processing - Compatible with standard AES implementations - Supports streaming and file-based media Implements the MediaBlock. classes.name: LiveSyncBlock
classes.summary: Live stream synchronization block that ensures frames are delivered on time for real-time streaming. The LiveSync block synchronizes live streams by managing frame timing, dropping late frames, and duplicating frames when needed to maintain consistent playback. This is essential for live streaming scenarios where maintaining real-time delivery is critical. Key features: - Real-time frame synchronization for live streams - Automatic dropping of late frames to prevent backlog - Frame duplication when frames arrive too late - Maintains consistent playback timing - Low-latency operation for live streaming - Suitable for live camera feeds, RTSP streams, and other real-time sources Common use cases: - Live camera streaming to ensure real-time delivery - RTSP stream synchronization for IP cameras - Live broadcasting to maintain consistent frame timing - Real-time video conferencing applications - Live sports or event streaming - Any scenario requiring strict real-time frame delivery Technical details: - Monitors frame timestamps and delivery timing - Drops frames that arrive too late to maintain real-time playback - Duplicates previous frame if current frame hasn't arrived yet - Operates with minimal latency for live scenarios - Handles format changes and events properly - Configurable latency and timeout parameters Implements the MediaBlock. classes.name: QueueBlock
classes.summary: A fundamental buffering block that provides thread decoupling and data buffering in media pipelines. The Queue block acts as a buffer between pipeline elements, allowing upstream and downstream components to operate at different rates and in different threads. classes.name: SRTPDecryptorBlock
classes.summary: A specialized media block that decrypts SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) streams in real-time. This block processes encrypted SRTP packets and outputs decrypted RTP packets, enabling secure media reception and playback of protected content. Key features: - SRTP decryption per RFC 3711 with configurable cipher suites - Support for AES-128-ICM and AES-256-ICM decryption - HMAC-SHA1 authentication verification with 80-bit or 32-bit tags - Real-time SRTP stream decryption with minimal latency - Transparent passthrough design for RTP/RTCP packets - Compatible with standard SRTP implementations - Separate decryption contexts for RTP and RTCP - Replay attack protection Common use cases: - Receiving secure VoIP and video conferencing streams - Decrypting real-time media broadcasts - Building secure streaming client applications with WebRTC - Implementing SIP/RTP security (SIPS/SRTP) receivers - Compliance with security regulations for real-time communications - Decrypting encrypted live video feeds and IP camera streams Technical details: - Uses AES decryption in Counter Mode (ICM/CTR) for low latency - Verifies message authentication and detects tampering - Maintains RTP timing and sequence numbers - Zero-copy operation where possible - Thread-safe decryption processing - Compatible with standard SRTP key exchange mechanisms (SDES, DTLS-SRTP) - Supports streaming and file-based media Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: TeeBlock
classes.summary: Provides a media stream splitter that duplicates input data to multiple outputs without modification.
classes.remarks: The (named after the Unix 'tee' command) acts as a 1-to-N splitter, taking a single input stream and replicating it to multiple output pads. This is essential for scenarios where the same media data needs to be processed or consumed by multiple downstream elements simultaneously. Key characteristics: Zero-copy operation - data is not duplicated in memoryMinimal performance overheadPreserves all stream properties (format, timing, metadata)Supports dynamic pad addition during pipeline operationEach output operates independently Common use cases: Recording while displaying videoApplying multiple different effects to the same sourceSending streams to multiple network destinationsCreating preview and high-quality encoding pathsImplementing A/B testing for processing chainsPerformance Note: While the tee itself has minimal overhead, connecting slow consumers can affect the entire pipeline. Consider using queue blocks after each tee output to decouple processing speeds. Failed outputs: an output whose downstream fails while streaming (it refuses a frame with a flow error) is cut off: it receives no further data until the next flush (a seek), the failure is reported through the pipeline's OnError, and the other outputs keep running. That holds while the pipeline is playing and another output still runs: a failure while the pipeline starts, or of the last running output, still stops it with an error. An element that posts its own error message still triggers the pipeline's error handling, and an output that reports end-of-stream still ends the stream. Requires GStreamer 1.28 or newer; with an older runtime a failed output stops every output of the tee.

constructors.name: TeeBlock
constructors.summary: Initializes a new instance of the TeeBlock class.
constructors.remarks: Creates a tee block with the specified number of output pads. Additional outputs can be added later using if needed. The media type determines what kind of data can flow through the tee: - For video streams - For audio streams - For any media type While you must specify at least one output during construction, unused outputs don't consume resources until connected. Queue settings control buffering behavior for each tee output. By default, low-latency settings are used (max 1 buffer per queue). Use for standard behavior. The defaults exist so the block catalog and the JSON pipeline persistence layer can construct a tee: TeeQueueSettings is the only settings type reachable from this constructor, and it is shared with QueueBlock, so the output count and the media type cannot be carried in a pipeline document. A restored tee always comes back with two Auto outputs; set them explicitly in code when a different shape is needed.

methods.summary: Dynamically adds a new output pad to the tee while the pipeline is running.
methods.remarks: This method allows adding outputs to a tee block during active pipeline operation without interrupting the media flow. This is useful for: Adding recording capabilities on demandConnecting monitoring or analysis tools dynamicallyImplementing dynamic routing scenarios The new pad inherits the media type of the tee block and can be immediately connected to downstream elements. Thread Safety: This method is thread-safe and can be called while the pipeline is in PLAYING state.
methods.returns: The newly created MediaBlockPad, or null if creation failed.

methods.name: RemovePadLive
methods.summary: Removes an output that was added at runtime by AddNewPadLive, taking its queue element out of the pipeline and handing the tee's request pad back with Pad) while the pipeline keeps running.
methods.remarks: Only live-added outputs can be removed. Build-time outputs are index-aligned with the tee's queues and with Outputs, and removing one would shift every output after it. Without this call, a tee that outlives its consumers strands one request pad and one queue element in the running pipeline per , and a stop/start rebuilds a branch for every entry that was never removed. The input this output fed is treated on a restart as after (#3976). This call blocks: it stops the branch's dataflow and waits for it to go idle, for up to two seconds. Do not call it from a GStreamer streaming thread or a pad probe - there the wait can only be satisfied by the calling thread itself returning, so the call always times out and the removal is refused.
methods.returns: true if the output was removed; false otherwise - the branch stays in the pipeline and keeps receiving data.

classes.name: CustomVideoEncoderBlock
classes.summary: Custom video encoder block for integrating third-party or specialized video encoders into the media pipeline. This block provides a flexible framework for adding GStreamer video encoder elements that are not directly supported by the SDK, enabling integration of proprietary codecs, experimental encoders, or platform-specific encoding solutions. Features automatic color space conversion to I420 format and dynamic property configuration through a key-value interface. Key features: - Integration of any GStreamer-compatible video encoder - Automatic video format conversion to I420 - Dynamic property configuration via dictionary - Support for hardware and software encoders - Custom codec parameter tuning - Plugin-based encoder extensions Common use cases: - Proprietary codec integration (custom H.264 variants) - Hardware-specific encoders (vendor SDKs) - Experimental codec testing (AV2, VVC) - Legacy format support (RealVideo, Indeo) - Specialized compression (lossless, HDR) - Custom streaming encoders The block handles the complexity of GStreamer element creation and pipeline integration while providing a simple configuration interface for encoder-specific parameters. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: D3D11DownloadBlock
classes.summary: Direct3D 11 memory download block for transferring GPU texture data to system memory. This Windows-specific block provides high-performance memory transfer from Direct3D 11 texture resources to CPU-accessible system memory. It handles the complex GPU-to-CPU synchronization, staging texture management, and efficient data copying required for Direct3D 11 interoperability. Features include support for various DXGI formats, automatic format conversion when needed, proper handling of multisampled textures, and optimal memory alignment for CPU access. Essential for screen capture applications, video processing pipelines that need CPU access to GPU-rendered content, computer vision systems processing GPU-accelerated video, and any Windows application requiring efficient readback of Direct3D 11 rendered or decoded video frames. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

methods.name: GetDefaultSettings
methods.summary: Gets the optimal default H.264 encoder settings based on available hardware acceleration. Automatically selects the best available encoder: hardware-accelerated encoders are preferred over software implementations for optimal performance.
methods.remarks: On Android and the Apple platforms the platform encoder is assumed when GStreamer is not initialized yet: the probe behind it is ElementFactory.Find, which throws before InitSDK, and an output constructed that early has always worked on these platforms. The same assumption AACEncoderBlock.GetDefaultSettings() makes about AVENC, for the same reason. The consequence is that the OpenH264 fallback is only reachable after InitSDK. An output constructed before it latches the platform encoder unprobed, and on a runtime that genuinely has none - a stripped framework, an Android image with no MediaCodec H.264 - the pipeline then fails to build rather than falling back. That is the behaviour macOS has always shipped, where the MP4 default was a hardcoded AppleMediaH264EncoderSettings with no probe at all; it is not new, only wider. Construct outputs after InitSDK to get the probe. On the other platforms a call before InitSDK returns OpenH264: there is no element registry to read yet, and with the redist in its deployed folder the lookup itself would throw. A warning goes to the trace log. The Windows output types call this on the first read of their Video property, so an output constructed before InitSDK still gets the GPU encoder if that read comes after it. calls it in the constructor, so it stays on OpenH264 when constructed before InitSDK. A GPU encoder is chosen because its GStreamer element exists. That does not prove it can encode right now: all NVENC sessions can be taken, or the driver can refuse. Call to find out, or set OpenH264 explicitly. NVENC, AMF and QSV come back with a keyframe every 25 frames rather than their own defaults, the cadence OpenH264 has, so the interval does not depend on which of those four gets picked.
methods.returns: The optimal H.264 encoder settings for the current system.

methods.name: CanEncodeAsync
methods.summary: Encodes a few test frames with the encoder these settings select, to find out whether it can really encode on this machine. IH264EncoderSettings) only says that its element exists.
methods.remarks: The answer holds for this moment and for a small frame. A session limit reached later, or a frame size the encoder refuses, can still fail a real encode. A check that runs out of its 15 seconds returns false and leaves its thread and pipeline behind, so don't repeat it in a loop: an encoder that wedged can keep hold of what a recording would need.
