methods.name: UpdateSettings
methods.summary: Updates the chroma key settings dynamically during runtime. Allows real-time adjustment of all chroma key parameters including color selection, sensitivity, edge refinement, and compositing quality without rebuilding the pipeline.

parameters.name: settings
parameters.summary: The new chroma key configuration settings to apply.

methods.name: Validated
methods.summary: Checks the settings this block cannot work without and hands them back.
methods.remarks: The keying filter builds its caps string from the source resolution, so settings without one can only fail inside Build - after a document has already materialized and reported success. A block whose Build returns false aborts CreatePipeline, so the whole pipeline then refuses to start, naming nothing but the block. Refusing the settings here makes the materializer report MBS040 naming the missing property instead. A zero or negative extent is refused for the same reason and is not a theoretical case: the size a document carries is read by SizeJsonConverter, which fills a missing or misspelled width or height with zero rather than failing, and caps of width=0 simply never negotiate.

parameters.name: settings
parameters.summary: The chroma key configuration settings to check.

methods.returns: The same settings instance.

methods.name: PublishChain
methods.summary: Points the block's output at output and claims the built latch, unless CleanUp has run since this build started. GitHub issue #957.
methods.remarks: The compare and the _isBuilt write are one critical section: the give-up path in CleanUp does its work while this thread still holds the gate, so without the compare its two writes are undone right here and every later Build() short-circuits on a block that owns nothing. The pad publish stays outside that lock. SetInternalPad blocks on RemoveProbe, which waits for an in-flight EOS probe, and that probe raises OnEOS on the streaming thread - a handler reading the effect count would take this lock. It does not make such a handler free to mutate the block: everything that mutates waits on _mutationGate, which this build holds. RefreshOutputPad publishes it under the same gate. It also stays ahead of the latch, where it has always been. Both orders were tried and neither has a reachable failure - AddProbe reports a failed install by returning 0 rather than throwing, and a discarded build leaving the pad on a chain it disowns costs nothing _inputPad does not already cost on every build. Do not move it again.

methods.name: MarkTornDown
methods.summary: Records that a teardown happened: the block is not built, and a build in flight has to discard rather than publish. GitHub issue #957.
methods.remarks: One critical section because the two writes are one fact. CleanUp reaches it from both paths - the give-up one, which runs while a build still holds the gate and is why the generation exists, and the ordinary one, which cannot race a build but has to mean the same to a build that started before either.

methods.name: TornDownSince
methods.summary: Whether a teardown has moved the block on since generation was read, so an insertion still in flight has to stop instead of reaching the graph. GitHub issue #960.
methods.remarks: Read without _videoEffectsLock on purpose: BaseVideoEffectFilter) asks this from inside an entry's monitor, and taking the list lock under one is the nesting no path in this class does - see EventArgs). The volatile read is not what makes the answer trustworthy, and it is worth being clear about which half is: the give-up path in CleanUp moves the generation BEFORE it sweeps the entries, and that sweep needs the same monitor the splice holds, so an BaseVideoEffectFilter) that takes the monitor after the sweep released it acquires the lock the sweeper exited - a barrier both threads passed through - and cannot miss the bump. What the volatile read adds is only that the value is re-read at all rather than cached in a register. != rather than >, the same as : the question is whether this is still the same run, not how many have been since.

parameters.name: generation
parameters.summary: The generation the caller snapshotted before it started.

methods.returns: true when MarkTornDown has run since.

methods.name: DiscardBuild
methods.summary: Gives back the filters a build published into the entries, for a build that lost the race with CleanUp's give-up path. GitHub issue #957.
methods.remarks: Exactly what the give-up path in CleanUp does and no more: drop the entries' filter references, touch no element. The elements belong to the pipeline, which is being disposed and releases its own children. The converter reference is kept, as that path also keeps it. The pipeline calls a second time from its dispose, while the pipeline is still alive - ClearData disposes it only after the per-block loop - and that call is what takes the converter to NULL and releases its wrapper. The pads likewise keep pointing at the discarded chain; the next build re-points them.

methods.name: AddOrUpdateAsync
methods.summary: Adds a new video effect or updates an existing effect in the processing chain. Supports dynamic effect modification during playback with automatic pipeline reconfiguration.
methods.remarks: Updating a name with an effect of a different type replaces the filter in the graph, so what is playing always matches what was last passed in. On a paused pipeline that replacement waits for playback to resume, and the previous filter stays in the graph until then. A wait that gives up after thirty seconds keeps the previous filter until the pipeline stops, and the next start applies the new effect. Reconfiguring a running graph is synchronous work, and this call does it on the thread it is called on - it can hold that thread for up to about three seconds while the pipeline pauses and resumes around the change. Awaiting does not move it elsewhere: when the effect has to wait for a pipeline that is starting or paused, the same work runs when the call resumes, which is on the calling thread again, after a wait of up to thirty seconds each time the call finds the pipeline not playing. Call this off the UI thread if a pause of that length would be visible.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.summary: The video effect to add or update.

methods.returns: A Task representing the asynchronous operation.

methods.name: RegisterAsync
methods.summary: Registers effect (or stores new settings for a registered one) without touching a graph that is already built: no filter is spliced in, an existing filter keeps its settings, and the next Build creates the filter from the stored effect. Replacing a name that is in the running graph with an effect that needs a filter of its own - another effect type, or a sample grabber the one in the graph cannot serve - is refused, since that would have to retire its filter. For callers that refuse a live change - a frame-size effect on a running pipeline - but keep the effect for the next start. Setting a property on an effect object that is already in the graph still applies live through its update event, and a new sample grabber instance the filter in the graph can serve takes its frames over at once.
methods.returns: true when the list now holds effect under its name.

methods.name: Attach
methods.summary: Attaches filter to the running graph as the filter of entry. The caller holds _mutationGate and hands over ownership of the filter: from here it is either the entry's or disposed.
methods.remarks: Synchronous on purpose, and it must stay that way: it runs with _mutationGate held, and the gate is also taken synchronously by IBaseVideoEffect), Clear and Build. An await in here would post its continuation to the caller's synchronization context - this SDK does not use ConfigureAwait(false) - so an application that added an effect from its UI thread and then removed one from a button handler would block that thread on the gate, leaving the continuation that releases it queued behind the block. That is a frozen application, not a slow one.

parameters.name: entry
parameters.summary: The entry, which must not have a filter yet.

methods.name: DropFilter
methods.summary: Forgets the filter of entry without touching the element - for the cases where the element belongs to a pipeline that is already gone, so removing or disposing it would be a call on freed memory. The element dies with its pipeline; the wrapper's toggle ref keeps it alive until then.
methods.returns: true when there was a filter to forget.

methods.name: RetireFilter
methods.summary: Takes the filter of entry out of the graph and releases it. The caller holds _mutationGate.
methods.remarks: The entry's own lock spans the removal, which is what makes a property setter unable to reach a disposed element. The one thing it can hold up is a setter for this same effect, and only for as long as the removal takes; the streaming thread never takes this lock unless the application sets a property from a frame callback, which already blocks inside the removal's pad probe today.
methods.returns: true when the entry has no filter afterwards; false when the filter could not be removed and is still in the graph.

methods.name: RefreshOutputPad
methods.summary: Points _outputPad at the src pad of the last filter in the graph - or the converter's when there is none - after a live edit changed the tail of the chain. The caller holds _mutationGate and must not hold any entry's lock. A block that is not built keeps its pads: the next Build sets them itself, and teardown deliberately leaves them pointing at the old run. GitHub issue #929.

methods.name: GuardTailRemoval
methods.summary: Arms an on-demand output's drop probe ahead on the pad that is the chain's tail once entry has left - a no-op unless entry is the tail. Same contract as RefreshOutputPad.

methods.name: TailSrcPad
methods.summary: The src pad of the chain's tail - the last filter in the graph, or the converter when there is none - with skip left out. RefreshOutputPad and GuardTailRemoval both go by it; a live add anchors its splice on its own.

parameters.name: skip
parameters.summary: An entry to leave out, or null.

methods.returns: The pad, or null when the tail has none.

methods.name: LastFilterInChainBefore
methods.summary: The last filter before stop - or in the whole list when it is null - whose elements are still in the graph: a retirement that failed after already nulling the filter's output element must yield neither a splice anchor nor the chain's tail, or the walk dereferences null. This is a field test, not a linkage test - a filter stuck in the bin with a severed link is still returned, and deliberately so: anchoring on it makes the next splice fail loudly, where skipping it would splice at the wrong position and silently invert the order.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.summary: The entry to stop in front of, or null for the whole list.

parameters.name: skip
parameters.summary: An entry whose filter is leaving, or null; only its Retiring one counts.

methods.returns: The filter, or null when only the converter is left.

methods.name: TryReadPipelineState
methods.summary: Reads the pipeline's state without touching a context or a wrapper that is on its way out.
methods.remarks: Every field on the way to the state can be nulled by a teardown running on another thread - MediaBlock.Dispose nulls the context itself, and ClearData nulls the pipeline - so each is read once into a local rather than re-read per dereference. The handle is checked before the state because CurrentState is an unchecked read at an offset from it: on a disposed wrapper that is an access violation, which cannot be caught, while Handle is a plain field read that is IntPtr.Zero by then. That narrows the window to the gap between these two lines; it does not close it.

methods.name: RemoveEntry
methods.summary: Takes the filter of entry out of the graph and the entry out of the list. A filter that could not be removed is still in the graph, so its entry stays in the list too - the two say the same thing. The caller holds _mutationGate.
methods.returns: true when the entry left the list.

methods.name: RemovalWaitsForPlaying
methods.summary: Whether a removal of the filter of entry has to wait for Playing, and if so marks the entry Removed. The caller holds _mutationGate. A removal of any kind overtakes a replacement still waiting.
methods.remarks: Taking a filter out of a built graph that is not playing needs a flush, and a frame that flush catches in the sink's preroll returns FLUSHING to the queue and the source behind the block, whose tasks then stay paused for good: the sink never prerolls again and the pipeline never reaches Playing. On a playing graph the removal waits for an idle pad instead. GitHub issue #3961.
methods.returns: true when the entry is left for RetireRemovedWhenPlayingAsync.

methods.name: StartRemovalWait
methods.summary: Starts RetireRemovedWhenPlayingAsync unless it is already waiting; one waiter takes out every entry marked removed. The caller holds _mutationGate.

methods.name: RetireRemovedWhenPlayingAsync
methods.summary: Takes out the entries Remove and Clear left in a graph that was not playing, once it plays. Nothing waits on it, so it has no timeout: a stop ends it, and CleanUp drops those entries instead. GitHub issue #3961.
methods.returns: A Task representing the asynchronous operation.

methods.name: RetireRemovedWhenPlayingCoreAsync
methods.summary: The loop of RetireRemovedWhenPlayingAsync.
methods.returns: A Task representing the asynchronous operation.

methods.name: RemoveWaitedEntry
methods.summary: EffectEntry) for the waiter, which has no caller to report to: a failure is reported here, and one entry failing does not keep the waiter from the others. The caller holds _mutationGate.

methods.name: SettleForNextBuild
methods.summary: Settles what a paused graph left open on an entry with no filter left in the graph: a replacement whose wait gave up becomes the entry's effect for the next Build, and otherwise a removal still waiting for Playing takes the entry out - a replacement is always the later call. CleanUp calls it once a retire succeeded, and BuildChain once it has dropped a filter the stop could not retire. The caller holds _mutationGate. GitHub issue #3961.
methods.returns: true when the entry left the list.

methods.summary: Finds the entry carrying name.
methods.returns: The entry, or null.

methods.returns: A snapshot of the entries, in order.

methods.name: HasFilter
methods.summary: Whether the entry currently has a filter in the graph.
methods.returns: true when a filter is attached.

methods.name: NeedsNewFilter
methods.summary: Whether effect replacing previous needs a filter of its own rather than new settings on the one in the graph: another type does, and so does a sample grabber - another instance or the same one with changed settings - whose Format or AllowFrameModification the grabber in the graph cannot serve: it reads both once, in IBaseVideoEffect}). One it can serve takes the frames over through the filter's handler, which follows the entry's effect. GitHub issues #3137, #3221.
methods.returns: true when the filter has to be replaced.

methods.name: Debug_Effects
methods.summary: The effects and what each of them has in the graph. For tests: the public API can only report the list, and the whole point of this class is that the two now agree.
methods.returns: One snapshot per registered effect, in order.

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Releases unmanaged and - optionally - managed resources.

parameters.name: disposing
parameters.summary: true to release both managed and unmanaged resources; false to release only unmanaged resources.

methods.name: ForgetEffects
methods.summary: Drops every effect and unsubscribes its handler, so a disposed block leaves no delegate behind in effects the application still holds.
methods.remarks: Takes only _videoEffectsLock, never the gate: the filters are CleanUp's to retire, and this has to stay reachable when the gate is wedged - see Boolean). The whole drain is one critical section, and the latch is set inside it. Draining a snapshot and then unsubscribing outside the lock is not enough, and neither is subscribing atomically on the other side: on the very path this method exists for - a mutation holding the gate past CleanUpGateTimeout, so gave up and returned - that mutation is still running, and it publishes its effect *after* this drain has been and gone. The entry was never in the snapshot, so nothing unsubscribes it, and the application is left holding a delegate into a disposed block. Only a latch the publisher also reads closes that, which is why the two share this lock rather than being ordered against each other. GitHub issue #957. Unsubscribing under the lock is free: OnUpdate is a field-like event, so -= is an interlocked delegate remove and runs no application code.

methods.name: CleanUp
methods.summary: Releases all resources and performs cleanup operations for this video effects block. This method takes every filter back out of the graph and disposes the video converter. The effects themselves stay registered, so a rebuild restores the chain.

classes.name: EffectEntry
classes.summary: One effect and the filter that carries it in the graph.
classes.remarks: The filter used to live in a second list inside VideoEffectsProcessor, and the two could not be mutated together - anything reaching GStreamer has to run outside the list lock. Keeping them in one object removes the question: there is no pair to disagree, and Filter being null is simply "registered, not in the graph". The entry is its own monitor for that field, so applying settings to the filter and retiring it are mutually exclusive and a property setter can never reach a disposed element. GitHub issue #926.

methods.summary: Tells whether blockPad is one this mixer handed out from AddInputPadLive and would therefore accept in MediaBlockPad).
methods.remarks: For a caller that has to tell a refusal meaning "this is not my pad" from one meaning "the removal did not complete": MediaBlockPad) reports both as false, and a build-time pad has to be released a different way while a refused live one must not be touched at all - it is still on the mixer, still in this list, and releasing it behind the mixer's back is the defect the removal API exists to avoid.

methods.name: IsLiveInputPad
methods.summary: The Pad overload of MediaBlockPad), for a caller that resolved a raw pad off the element and has no MediaBlockPad for it.
methods.remarks: A raw pad resolved by ordinal can land on any input, live ones included - GStreamer does not order Element.Pads. Releasing such a pad directly would hand back an input the mixer still lists, and its own later removal would release it a second time.
methods.returns: true when the pad belongs to a live-added input of this mixer.

methods.name: RemoveInputPadLive
methods.summary: Removes an input that was added at runtime by AddInputPadLive, handing the mixer's request pad back with Pad) while the pipeline keeps running.
methods.remarks: Only live-added inputs can be removed. Build-time inputs are index-aligned with the mixer's configured streams, and removing one would shift every configured stream after it; AddInputPadLive adds no stream entry, which is what makes its inputs removable. This call blocks: it stops the input's dataflow and waits for the upstream to go idle, for up to two seconds. Do not call it from a GStreamer streaming thread or a pad probe - there the wait can only be satisfied by the calling thread itself returning, so the call always times out and the removal is refused.

classes.name: D3D11VideoCompositorBlock
classes.summary: Direct3D 11 hardware-accelerated video compositor block for multi-stream video mixing. This Windows-specific block provides GPU-accelerated video compositing using Direct3D 11, enabling real-time mixing of multiple video streams with exceptional performance. Features include per-stream positioning and scaling, alpha blending and transparency, chroma key (green screen) support, animated transitions with fade in/out effects, z-order layering, and hardware-accelerated color space conversion. The compositor efficiently handles multiple HD/4K streams using GPU resources, making it ideal for live production systems, video conferencing with multiple participants, virtual sets, picture-in-picture layouts, video walls, and professional broadcast applications. Requires Windows 8+ and Direct3D 11 compatible GPU. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: D3D11VideoConverterBlock
classes.summary: Direct3D 11 video converter block that provides hardware-accelerated video format conversion and color space transformation. This block leverages Direct3D 11 Video API for GPU-based video processing, offering superior performance compared to software-based converters. It supports a wide range of pixel formats including YUV formats (NV12, I420, YUY2, UYVY) and RGB formats, with automatic color space conversion between them. Key features: - Hardware-accelerated format conversion using GPU resources - Minimal CPU usage for high-performance video pipelines - Support for HDR (High Dynamic Range) video processing - Automatic handling of video stride and alignment requirements - Zero-copy operations when possible for optimal memory efficiency Common use cases: - Converting camera/capture formats to encoder-friendly formats (e.g., RGB to NV12) - Preparing video for Direct3D 11 rendering or processing - High-performance video transcoding pipelines - Real-time video streaming applications - Integration with Windows Media Foundation encoders Requirements: - Windows 7 or later with Direct3D 11 capable GPU - DirectX 11 runtime and appropriate GPU drivers - Hardware video acceleration support (DXVA2) Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: D3D12FisheyeDewarpBlock
classes.summary: Direct3D 12 block that dewarps a fisheye image on the GPU into an equirectangular, panorama or perspective view, set by Projection. The view (rotation, field of view, region of interest, viewport) can be changed while the pipeline runs: change Settings and call Update. The output has the input's size, format and frame rate; add a resize block after it for another size. The block moves frames to and from the GPU itself: its input and its output each take system, D3D11 or D3D12 memory, whichever the neighbouring block uses, and D3D12 memory on the block's own adapter passes through without a copy on both sides. Requires a Direct3D 12 capable GPU. CVDewarpBlock is the CPU alternative. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals.

classes.name: D3D12InterlaceBlock
classes.summary: Direct3D 12 block that converts progressive video to interlaced video on the GPU. This is the opposite of deinterlacing: the input must be progressive, and the output is interleaved interlaced video with the field order set by TopFieldFirst. The output frame rate follows from the input rate and FieldPattern. The block moves frames to and from the GPU itself: its input and its output each take system, D3D11 or D3D12 memory, whichever the neighbouring block uses, and D3D12 memory on the block's own adapter passes through without a copy on both sides. The output can be linked only to a consumer that accepts interlaced video. Requires a Direct3D 12 capable GPU. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals.

classes.name: D3D12RemapBlock
classes.summary: Direct3D 12 block that remaps the video on the GPU through a UV map: every output point shows the input point the map gives for it, which covers lens calibration, warping and any other geometric transformation. The map (Map) can be replaced while the pipeline runs: change Settings and call Update. The block uploads the map to the GPU the frames are on and owns the GPU copy; the application never handles a Direct3D resource. The output has the input's size, format and frame rate; add a resize block after it for another size. The block moves frames to and from the GPU itself: its input and its output each take system, D3D11 or D3D12 memory, whichever the neighbouring block uses, and D3D12 memory passes through without a copy on both sides. Requires a Direct3D 12 capable GPU. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals.

classes.name: VideoEffectsWinBlock
classes.summary: Video effects processing block for Windows that applies real-time visual effects to video streams. This block leverages Windows Media Foundation (MFP) for high-performance video effect processing, supporting a wide range of effects including image overlays, text rendering, scrolling text, color adjustments, transformations, and custom GPU effects. Effects are applied sequentially in the order they are added, allowing for complex effect chains. Key features: - Hardware-accelerated effect processing using Windows Media Foundation - Support for multiple simultaneous effects with minimal performance impact - Dynamic effect management (add, remove, update during playback) - Frame-accurate effect timing and positioning - Thread-safe effect list management for real-time modifications - Automatic resource management and disposal Supported effect types: - Image overlays (logos, watermarks, picture-in-picture) - Text overlays with rich formatting options - Scrolling text effects (tickers, credits) - Color correction and grading - Geometric transformations (rotate, scale, crop) - Custom shader-based effects Common use cases: - Adding branding/watermarks to video streams - Real-time text overlay for live streaming (timestamps, titles) - Video production with dynamic graphics - Security video with timestamp and camera ID overlays - Educational content with annotations - Broadcasting with lower-thirds and graphics Performance considerations: - Effects are processed on BGR frames - GPU acceleration when available through MFP - Efficient memory management with frame reuse - Optimized for real-time processing at 60+ FPS Requirements: - Windows 7 or later - Windows Media Foundation runtime - DirectX 9 or later for GPU acceleration Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

classes.name: VideoRendererBlock
classes.summary: Cross-platform video renderer block providing display output for video streams. This block serves as the final destination for video in a media pipeline, rendering frames to various display surfaces across different platforms and UI frameworks. Features include hardware-accelerated rendering using platform-specific APIs (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL ES on mobile, Metal on Apple platforms), support for multiple UI frameworks (WPF, WinForms, MAUI, WinUI, Android Views, iOS/macOS views), subtitle overlay rendering, snapshot capture functionality, frame stepping, and playback rate control. The renderer automatically selects the optimal rendering path based on the platform and UI framework, providing native performance while maintaining a consistent API. Essential for media players, video editors, streaming clients, video conferencing apps, and any application requiring high-quality video display with minimal latency. Implements the MediaBlock. Implements the IMediaBlockInternals. Implements the IDisposable.

constructors.name: VideoRendererBlock
constructors.summary: Initializes a new instance of the VideoRendererBlock class that draws into a window the caller owns, rather than into a VideoView.
constructors.remarks: Windows: this constructor defaults to D3D11VideoRendererSettings (d3d11videosink), the same as the VideoView constructor. Assigning a plain selects the OpenGL renderer (glimagesink) instead. Windows:d3d11videosink attaches to by posting a message to the window and waiting until the window's own thread processes it. That thread must keep pumping messages while the pipeline starts - do not block it waiting on the pipeline - and the window must belong to this process. macOS: must be an NSView*, not an NSWindow*. This constructor defaults to MetalVideoRendererSettings, and the Metal sink takes the handle as a view and sends it -bounds without a type check - an NSWindow* aborts the process with "unrecognized selector" on the first frame. macOS: the Metal renderer is the only one that honours the handle. Assigning a different after construction does not give you the same picture in the same view - it gives up the view. The renderer falls back to autovideosink, the handle is dropped, and a window of its own opens instead - with a Warning in the log saying so. The same happens if the installed redist has no vfmetalvideosink. So on macOS this is a choice between "renders into your view, on the Metal sink" and "renders somewhere else" - not a choice of renderer. macOS, and the reason this matters more here than for the VideoView constructor: the Metal sink attaches to the view through dispatch_sync on the MAIN queue. The host must therefore keep a Cocoa run loop servicing its main thread for as long as the pipeline runs. A host that creates an NSView and then blocks its main thread waiting on the pipeline will deadlock the streaming thread on the first frame. This constructor is the API for hosts with no managed view, which are the most likely to be shaped that way - hence the warning.

parameters.name: windowHandle
parameters.summary: The native window handle to render into: an HWND on Windows, an NSView* on macOS. On Android and iOS it is handed to the platform OpenGL renderer instead, and the constructor taking a VideoView is the supported path there - it reads the handle off the view, so the type is never the caller's to get right. Pass Zero to let the renderer open a window of its own.

classes.name: MediaPlayerCoreX
classes.summary: Cross-platform media player SDK built on a modern MediaBlocks pipeline architecture. Provides comprehensive media playback capabilities for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android platforms. Supports various media sources including files, network streams (RTSP, RTMP, HLS), IP cameras, and custom sources. Features include hardware-accelerated decoding, real-time effects processing, subtitle support, and multi-stream handling.
classes.remarks: This is the modern, cross-platform media player SDK recommended for new development projects. It replaces legacy platform-specific players and provides unified API across all supported platforms. Built on a cross-platform media framework for maximum format compatibility and MediaBlocks for modular pipeline construction.

methods.name: Audio_Effects_AddOrUpdate
methods.summary: Adds a new audio effect to the pipeline or updates an existing effect with the same name. The effect is applied in real-time to the audio stream during playback without interrupting the media. If an effect with the same name already exists, its parameters will be updated with the new values. Effects are processed in the order they were added to the pipeline.
methods.remarks: This method supports dynamic audio effect management during playback. When updating an existing effect, the audio stream will smoothly transition to the new effect parameters without artifacts. Effect names are used as unique identifiers, so ensure each effect has a distinct name if you want to apply multiple effects of the same type simultaneously. Effects live for one playback session: a stop, the end of the file or the next OpenAsync after a start that returned false discards them. An effect added after playback has stopped, ended or failed to start applies from the next OpenAsync and PlayAsync. With PauseOnStop the end of the file keeps the session open, so an effect added then belongs to it and the next OpenAsync discards it. Otherwise, adding one after the end of the file or a failed start closes the finished session on the calling thread, as the next OpenAsync would: its effects are discarded, its duration, stream lists and snapshot are no longer available, and playing again needs OpenAsync first. A source error during playback, including a file or URL that fails after PlayAsync returned true, also keeps the session open. An effect added then is not applied, neither after ResumeAsync nor after the next OpenAsync, and no error is reported. Call StopAsync first, and the effect applies from the next OpenAsync.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.summary: The audio effect to add or update in the effects pipeline. Must not be null.

methods.name: Audio_Effects_Remove
methods.summary: Removes an audio effect from the pipeline by its instance. Once removed, the effect will no longer be applied to the audio stream. The audio processing will continue with the remaining active effects in the pipeline.
methods.remarks: This method disconnects the effect's update event handlers and removes it from the internal effects collection. If the effect is not found in the pipeline, this method completes without error. The audio stream will smoothly adapt to the removal without interruption. An effect that changes the channel count of the playing stream is not removed until playback stops, and an error is reported for it.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.summary: The audio effect instance to remove from the pipeline. Must not be null.

methods.name: Audio_Effects_Clear
methods.summary: Clears all audio effects from the pipeline, returning audio processing to the original unmodified stream. This method removes all active audio effects and resets the audio processing chain to its default state. The audio playback continues without interruption using the original, unprocessed audio signal.
methods.remarks: This method is useful when you want to quickly disable all audio processing and return to the original audio. All effect update event handlers are disconnected and the effects are cleared from the pipeline. The operation completes smoothly without audio artifacts. An effect that changes the channel count of the playing stream stays until playback stops, and an error is reported for it.

methods.summary: Best-effort dispose helper. Casts to IDisposable (most MediaBlocks implement it) and swallows exceptions so a single failing block can't abort the rest of the teardown. Calling Dispose on a block already disposed by the pipeline is a no-op thanks to MediaBlock's idempotent disposed-value guard. Made non-static so failures route through the player's Context (Serilog / Android Log) rather than disappearing into Trace.

Called on the teardown path to stop the bus thread from invoking handlers on a player that is mid-dispose — StopAsync/SetState(Null) can still fire OnStop / OnBusStreamCollection while we're already tearing down _ctx, and those handlers reference _videoView and raise public events that the host may have detached.

methods.name: Dispose
methods.summary: Releases unmanaged and - optionally - managed resources.
methods.remarks: Exception-safe teardown: the body is wrapped in a try/finally so the log sink is flushed and the completion source published even when CloseX or DisposeCore throws. On success disposedValue is set; on a fault it is deliberately left false and the completion slot re-armed, so a later explicit Boolean) retries the teardown — the same policy as VideoCaptureCoreX / SimplePlayerCoreX.

parameters.name: disposing
parameters.summary: true to release both managed and unmanaged resources; false to release only unmanaged resources.

methods.name: DisposeCore
methods.summary: Disposes the core.

parameters.name: disposing
parameters.summary: Always true on every path that reaches this method today: Boolean) returns before it when called from the finalizer (issue #840), and DisposeAsync passes true. The rest is the safety contract any future caller passing false inherits: we must NOT take _additionalAudioStreamsLock — if another thread was inside an Audio_AdditionalStreams_* mutator at the moment the object became collectible, taking the lock on the finalizer thread would deadlock GC. Since the object is already unreachable at finalization, skipping the clear is safe: the List itself will be reclaimed by GC along with the parent. Managed wrappers are released on the disposing path only: their public Dispose()s route to their disposing:true branches (_videoCompositionManager → Clear(), which disposes GstSharp wrappers), and running that on the finalizer thread can deadlock the finalizer queue or use-after-free inside the binding — the exact hazard VideoCompositionManager.Dispose documents for itself. Both wrappers own their finalizers, so skipping them here still releases the native side.

On success disposedValue is set; on a fault it is deliberately left false, the completion slot is re-armed and the latch flags reset, so a subsequent Dispose/DisposeAsync retries the teardown — the same policy as VideoCaptureCoreX / SimplePlayerCoreX.

methods.remarks: The rate is the pipeline's. A positive rate set before playback starts, while it is starting, or while parked at the end (PauseOnStop) is stored and applied when playback next starts. A forward rate survives that pause-at-end replay. After the media ends or after Stop, the next play is at 1.0; set the rate again after OpenAsync. methods.name: NextFrame
methods.summary: Advances the video playback by exactly one frame in the current playback direction. This method pauses the player and moves by a single frame, useful for precise video analysis or frame-by-frame examination. The operation requires a video renderer to be present and only works with seekable sources like media files, not live streams.
methods.remarks: Frame stepping behavior: - Automatically pauses playback before stepping to ensure precise control - During reverse playback steps one frame backwards; the playback rate is not changed - Requires a video renderer to be configured in the player - Only works with seekable media sources (files), not live streams Use this method for precise video analysis, educational content, or debugging purposes.
methods.returns: true if the frame step operation was successful; false if it failed due to missing video renderer or unsupported source.

methods.name: PrevFrame
methods.summary: Steps by exactly one frame against the current playback direction. This method moves the playback position by a single frame using seek operations, useful for precise frame-by-frame video analysis. The operation requires seekable video content and may be slower than NextFrame because it seeks.
methods.remarks: Frame stepping limitations and behavior: - During forward playback steps one frame backwards and sets the playback rate to 1.0 - During reverse playback steps one frame forwards and keeps the reverse rate - Requires a valid pipeline and at least one video stream - Only works with seekable media sources (files), not live streams - Uses seek operations which may be slower than forward stepping - Accuracy depends on the underlying codec's ability to seek to exact frames - May not work reliably with all video formats or codecs - Performance varies based on video compression and keyframe intervals This method is primarily intended for video analysis and educational purposes where precise frame-by-frame navigation is needed.
methods.returns: true if the frame step was successful; false if it failed due to missing pipeline, no video streams, or seek limitations.

methods.name: Audio_Stream_Select
methods.summary: Switches to a different audio stream in multi-stream media content. This method allows dynamic switching between audio tracks during playback, commonly used for multi-language content or content with multiple audio channels (commentary, music, etc.). The switch occurs seamlessly without interrupting video playback.
methods.remarks: Audio stream switching behavior: - Maintains current video stream while switching audio - Sends a SELECT_STREAMS event to the underlying media pipeline - Works during active playback without interruption - Requires the media to contain multiple audio streams - The target stream must be available in the current media content Use this method for implementing audio track selection in media players with multi-language or multi-channel content.

parameters.name: stream
parameters.summary: The target audio stream to switch to. Must be a valid AudioStreamInfo from the media's available audio streams.

methods.returns: true if the audio stream was successfully switched; false if the operation failed due to invalid source, null stream, a stream with no ID, a source that cannot switch streams (anything but UniversalSourceSettings on the advanced engine without DisableHWDecoders and Blu-ray), or stream event failure.

methods.name: Video_Stream_Select
methods.summary: Switches to a different video stream in multi-stream media content. This method allows dynamic switching between video tracks during playback, useful for content with multiple video angles, resolutions, or different video content tracks. The switch occurs seamlessly while maintaining audio playback if present.
methods.remarks: Video stream switching behavior: - Maintains current audio stream while switching video - Sends a SELECT_STREAMS event to the underlying media pipeline - Works during active playback without stopping - Requires the media to contain multiple video streams - May cause brief visual interruption during the switch - The target stream must be available in the current media content Common use cases include multi-angle video content, adaptive bitrate streaming, or educational content with multiple camera views.

parameters.name: stream
parameters.summary: The target video stream to switch to. Must be a valid VideoStreamInfo from the media's available video streams.

methods.returns: true if the video stream was successfully switched; false if the operation failed due to invalid source, null stream, a stream with no ID, a source that cannot switch streams (anything but UniversalSourceSettings on the advanced engine without DisableHWDecoders and Blu-ray), or stream event failure.

methods.remarks: Blocks must be registered before the pipeline is built; calling this while the engine is running (or after the pipeline has been built) is a no-op (logged as a warning). The block is inserted after the video effects and before the sample grabber, so its overlays reach both the renderer and every output. Once playback starts the block is owned by the playback pipeline and is disposed when playback stops; register a fresh block instance before each session. Subscribe to the block's own event to receive detections.

parameters.summary: The video processing block to add. Ignored when null or already added.

methods.name: Audio_Processing_AddBlock
methods.summary: Registers an audio processing block (e.g. the Whisper speech-to-text block) to be inserted into the audio chain on the next Play.
methods.remarks: The audio chain is only built when audio playback is active, so an audio source must be configured for the block to run. Same lifecycle as IVideoProcessingBlock): register before Play; the block is owned and disposed by the playback pipeline once started.

parameters.name: block
parameters.summary: The audio processing block to add. Ignored when null or already added.

methods.name: Audio_Processing_RemoveBlock

methods.returns: true if the block was registered and removed; otherwise false.

methods.name: DisposeRegisteredProcessingBlocksOnFailure
methods.summary: Disposes every registered processing block and clears the lists. Called on a failed pipeline build (any failure exit of CreatePipelineAsync, not just the exception path). Blocks already wired into the pipeline are disposed by ClearPipeline; re-disposing them here is a safe no-op because Dispose is idempotent. Blocks registered but never wired (the build failed before reaching them) are NOT owned by the pipeline, so disposing them here is what prevents their heavy native AI resources (ONNX / Whisper models) from leaking. The caller re-adds fresh blocks for the next session.

methods.name: DisposeUnwiredProcessingBlocks
methods.summary: Disposes and drops registered processing blocks whose host chain was NOT built this session, on a SUCCESSFUL build. A block registered for an inactive chain — a video block when the source has no video stream (_videoActive off), or an audio block when there is no audio source (_audioActive off) — is never wired into the pipeline, so the pipeline never owns or disposes it. The engine owns registered blocks, so it disposes the un-wired ones here to keep their native AI models from leaking (mirrors the failure-path DisposeRegisteredProcessingBlocksOnFailure). Blocks for a chain that WAS built are owned by the pipeline and left untouched. Disposes outside the lock.

parameters.name: videoChainBuilt
parameters.summary: True if the video chain (and its block-wiring loop) ran.

parameters.name: audioChainBuilt
parameters.summary: True if the audio chain (and its block-wiring loop) ran.

methods.name: Video_Effects_AddOrUpdateAsync
methods.summary: Asynchronously adds a new video effect to the pipeline or updates an existing effect with the same name. The effect is applied in real-time to the video stream without interrupting playback.
methods.remarks: Effects live for one playback session: a stop, the end of the file or the next OpenAsync after a start that returned false discards them. An effect added after playback has stopped, ended or failed to start applies from the next OpenAsync and PlayAsync. With PauseOnStop the end of the file keeps the session open, so an effect added then belongs to it and the next OpenAsync discards it. Otherwise, adding one after the end of the file or a failed start closes the finished session, as the next OpenAsync would: its effects are discarded, its duration, stream lists and snapshot are no longer available, and playing again needs OpenAsync first. A source error during playback, including a file or URL that fails after PlayAsync returned true, also keeps the session open. This call then waits up to 30 seconds for playback and reports an error. Unless ResumeAsync runs during that wait, the effect is not applied, and the next OpenAsync discards it. Call StopAsync first, and the effect applies from the next OpenAsync.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.summary: The video effect to add or update in the effects pipeline.

methods.returns: A task representing the asynchronous operation.

methods.name: Video_Effects_Get
methods.summary: Retrieves a video effect from the pipeline by its unique name.
methods.remarks: Once a session has stopped, ended or failed to start, this returns null for its effects, in an OnStop handler too, and returns an effect added since, for the next session. With PauseOnStop or after a source error the session stays open, and this still returns its effects. A PlayAsync that retries a failed start without OpenAsync runs the same session again, with its effects, although this returned null for them; to take one out of the retry, call String) or Video_Effects_ClearAsync.

parameters.name: effectName
parameters.summary: The name of the effect to retrieve.

methods.returns: The video effect instance if found; null otherwise.

methods.name: Video_Effects_RemoveAsync
methods.summary: Asynchronously removes a video effect from the pipeline. Temporarily pauses playback during removal to ensure smooth effect removal without artifacts.
methods.remarks: If the player cannot pause - it is already stopping, or disposed - the failure is logged and the effect is left in place rather than the call hanging. After the end of the file or a failed start nothing is paused: the effect is dropped and the session stays as it is.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.summary: The video effect instance to remove from the pipeline.

methods.returns: A task representing the asynchronous operation.

methods.name: Video_Effects_RemoveAsync
methods.summary: Removes a video effect by name asynchronously. Pauses playback during removal.
methods.remarks: If the player cannot pause - it is already stopping, or disposed - the failure is logged and the effect is left in place rather than the call hanging. After the end of the file or a failed start nothing is paused: the effect is dropped and the session stays as it is.

parameters.name: name
parameters.summary: The name of the effect to remove.

methods.returns: A Task representing the asynchronous operation.

methods.name: PauseForEffectRemovalAsync
methods.summary: Pauses playback before an effect is unplugged from the running graph.
methods.remarks: This used to poll while (State != Pause) with no bound, so a player that cannot pause never returned from the public removal call (GitHub issue #918). Polling was never the right shape for it: Pause assigns the state before it touches GStreamer, so once PauseAsync has completed the state has either moved or was never going to - the call bailed out early because the player is disposed, has no pipeline, or is already stopping. Reading it once answers the question that the loop could only ever answer by timing out. A player that was never opened has no pipeline to pause and drops the effect straight from the list.
methods.returns: true when the effect may be removed; false when the pause did not land.

methods.name: RestoreFileSegment
methods.summary: Downstream flush during remove drops the file SEGMENT. Seek restores it on VOD. Live sources have no duration — do not Flush-seek those.

methods.name: Video_Effects_Clear
methods.summary: Clears all video effects from the pipeline, returning video processing to the original unmodified stream.
methods.remarks: This method never changes the pipeline state - disposal calls it. It refuses to run while the pipeline is playing and a frame-size effect is registered; use Video_Effects_ClearAsync for the pausing variant.

methods.name: Video_Effects_ClearAsync
methods.summary: Clears all video effects from the pipeline asynchronously, pausing playback during removal.
methods.remarks: The pipeline is temporarily paused, the same discipline IBaseVideoEffect) uses. If the player cannot pause - it is already stopping, or disposed - the failure is logged and the effects are left in place rather than the call hanging. A frame-size effect present on a playing pipeline refuses the clear, the same rule the removal calls enforce. After the end of the file or a failed start nothing is paused: the effects are dropped and the session stays as it is.
methods.returns: A task representing the asynchronous operation.

classes.name: OnvifUdpClient
classes.summary: Provides a UDP client implementation specifically designed for ONVIF device discovery using the WS-Discovery protocol.
classes.remarks: This class wraps to provide ONVIF-specific functionality for sending WS-Discovery probe messages and receiving probe match responses from ONVIF devices. The client is configured with broadcast enabled to support multicast operations required by the WS-Discovery protocol. Each instance is bound to a specific local endpoint, typically representing a single network interface. This class implements and should be properly disposed after use to release network resources.

methods.name: Finalize

methods.remarks: The finalizer is called by the garbage collector when the object is no longer reachable. It ensures that unmanaged resources are released even if Dispose was not called explicitly. To avoid finalizer overhead, always call Dispose when you are done with the object.

methods.remarks: This method implements the IDisposable interface and should be called when the OnvifUdpClient is no longer needed. classes.remarks: This factory encapsulates the logic for creating properly configured instances bound to specific network interfaces. It supports both single-interface scenarios and multi-interface discovery where clients are created for all valid network adapters. The factory automatically filters out invalid network interfaces such as loopback adapters, interfaces that are down, or interfaces that don't support IPv4, ensuring efficient and reliable device discovery.

methods.name: CreateClient

methods.remarks: The created client is configured with broadcast enabled to support the multicast operations required by the WS-Discovery protocol used in ONVIF device discovery.

methods.summary: Creates UDP clients for all valid network interfaces available on the system.
methods.remarks: This method enumerates all network interfaces on the system and creates UDP clients only for interfaces that meet the following criteria: Interface type is Ethernet or Wireless (on non-Android platforms)Operational status is Up (interface is active)Interface supports IPv4 Socket exceptions that occur during client creation (e.g., due to permission issues or port conflicts) are caught and those clients are excluded from the returned collection. Creating clients for all interfaces ensures comprehensive device discovery across different network segments, which is particularly important in multi-homed systems or systems with multiple network adapters.

methods.name: IsValidAdapter

methods.remarks: An adapter is considered valid if it meets all of the following conditions: The interface type is Ethernet or Wireless (on non-Android platforms). This check is skipped on Android to accommodate platform-specific network interface naming.The operational status is Up (not Down, Testing, Unknown, etc.).The interface supports IPv4 communication. These checks help minimize discovery time by excluding interfaces that cannot participate in multicast UDP communication or are not currently active on the network.
methods.returns: true if the adapter meets all criteria for discovery operations; otherwise, false.

classes.name: Discovery
classes.summary: Provides ONVIF device discovery functionality using the WS-Discovery protocol.
classes.remarks: The Discovery class implements the ONVIF-compliant WS-Discovery protocol to locate ONVIF devices on the local network. It sends multicast probe messages to UDP port 3702 and collects responses from devices that support the ONVIF NetworkVideoTransmitter profile. The class automatically creates UDP clients for all available network interfaces to ensure comprehensive discovery across different network segments. Duplicate responses from the same device (identified by IP address) are automatically filtered. Two discovery patterns are supported: - Real-time callback: Devices are reported immediately as they respond via a callback action. - Batch collection: All devices are collected and returned after the timeout period expires.

None of them is an error: discovery goes on with the other interfaces. When the probe could not be sent on any interface, discovery throws a DiscoveryException instead.

methods.name: Discover
methods.summary: Discovers ONVIF devices on the network and invokes a callback for each unique device as responses arrive.
methods.remarks: This method is ideal for real-time discovery scenarios such as populating a UI list as devices respond. The callback runs on the thread pool, so it does not block the discovery loop, and callbacks for different devices can run concurrently. The returned task completes after every callback has returned, or when is cancelled. Devices are identified as unique by their IP address. If a device responds multiple times or from multiple interfaces, the callback will only be invoked once for that device.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.summary: The maximum duration in seconds to wait for device responses. Typical values range from 3 to 10 seconds.

parameters.name: onDeviceDiscovered

methods.returns: A task that completes when the timeout expires, cancellation is requested, or all network interfaces have finished listening.

methods.name: Discover
methods.summary: Discovers ONVIF devices on the network and returns a complete collection of all devices found within the timeout period.
methods.remarks: This method waits for the full timeout period to collect all device responses before returning the complete collection. For scenarios requiring immediate notification as devices respond, use the overload. The returned collection contains only unique devices, filtered by IP address. Each device will appear only once in the collection even if it responded multiple times or was detected through multiple network interfaces.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.summary: The maximum duration in seconds to wait for device responses. Typical values range from 3 to 10 seconds.

parameters.name: cancellationToken
parameters.summary: An optional cancellation token to stop the discovery process before the timeout expires.

methods.returns: A task that represents the asynchronous operation. The task result contains an enumerable collection of DiscoveryDevice instances, each representing a unique ONVIF device discovered on the network.

methods.name: Discover
methods.summary: Performs device discovery using a single UDP client bound to a specific network interface.
methods.remarks: This method sends a single WS-Discovery probe message and then enters a receive loop to collect responses until the timeout expires. A probe that cannot be sent ends discovery on this client at once. A failed receive is retried after a short pause, and a malformed response is skipped. The UDP client is always closed in the finally block.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.summary: The maximum duration in seconds to listen for device responses on this network interface.

parameters.name: client
parameters.summary: The UDP client bound to a specific network interface for sending probes and receiving responses.

parameters.name: onDeviceDiscovered
parameters.summary: The callback action to invoke when a valid device response is received and parsed.

parameters.name: cancellationToken
parameters.summary: The cancellation token to stop the discovery process.

methods.returns: A task that completes when the timeout expires, cancellation is requested, or the client is closed. Its result is the exception that stopped the probe from being sent, or null when the probe went out.

methods.remarks: The probe is sent to the WS-Discovery multicast address (239.255.255.250:3702) and includes the NetworkVideoTransmitter type filter to discover ONVIF-compliant video devices.
